g.acceptance-criteria.def: The checkable statements that define done — each one passes or fails. The bridge between a human’s intent and a machine’s instructions, and the test list written first.
g.accessibility.def: Building so people with disabilities can use the product: semantics, contrast, keyboard, screen readers. WCAG is the standard.
g.acid.def: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees transactions are designed to provide.
g.agent.def: A model plus a loop plus tools: it observes, plans, acts (reads files, runs commands, calls APIs), and repeats until it decides it is done. Agency multiplies both leverage and blast radius.
g.agent.steward: The loop is what makes an agent useful and what makes containment non-optional. Permissions are the difference between a tool and a hazard.
g.api.def: Application Programming Interface — a defined way for one piece of software to ask another for data or actions: endpoints, methods, inputs, outputs. It is a contract you can check, not a description you trust.
g.api.steward: Every API call an agent writes is a claim. Verify the method, the status codes, and what happens on retry against the real contract.
g.artifact.def: A concrete byproduct you can inspect: a diff, a test run, a log line, a screenshot, a database row. A “verifiable artifact” is one anyone can check independently — “it works” is an adjective, not an artifact.
g.atomic.def: Indivisible: it happens completely or not at all, with no gap for anything else to run. The property that makes read-modify-write safe and races impossible.
g.bandwidth.def: How much data can flow per second — as opposed to how long one exchange takes (latency). A big pipe with a long way to travel is still slow for interactive work.
g.caching.def: Storing a computed result for faster reuse — gaining speed at the risk of serving stale data. Cache invalidation is the part agents decide silently.
g.caching.steward: “I added caching for performance” is a trade you did not approve. Ask for the invalidation policy and who pays for stale data.
g.ci.def: Continuous Integration — automatically building and testing every change. The machine checking the machine, with no opinions and no mercy.
g.code-review.def: Reading a change for correctness and risk before it merges. The human gate that makes agent-speed development survivable.
g.cohesion.def: How focused a module’s responsibilities are. High cohesion means the refund rule lives in one place you can find.
g.compiler.def: A program that checks and translates source before it runs. It verifies that code is well-formed, not that it is correct.
g.concurrency.def: Making progress on multiple tasks by interleaving them — not the same as parallelism (executing at the same instant).
g.constraint.def: A rule the system enforces by itself: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK in a database; bounds and types in code. Constraints make invalid states impossible instead of relying on everyone to remember.
g.context-window.def: The fixed token budget a model can attend to in one call: prompt, rules, open files, tool output, and its own answer all compete for it. When it fills, instructions decay — studies find models lose material in the middle.
g.context-window.steward: Short, fresh sessions with a written spec beat one long conversation. Context is a resource you spend, not a container that remembers.
g.cookie.def: A small piece of data the server asks the browser to store and send back on later requests — the basis of sessions, and the reason CSRF matters.
g.cors.def: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — the browser rules that decide whether a page may read a response from another origin. It is configured by the server; the client cannot fix it.
g.cors.steward: The dangerous “fix” is reflecting any Origin with credentials allowed. The correct fix is an allowlist of trusted origins.
g.coupling.def: How much one module depends on another’s internals. Lower coupling means changes stay local instead of rippling.
g.coverage.def: Which lines of code ran during tests. Useful as a map of what was never executed — not as evidence of correctness.
g.csp.def: A response header that lists what a page may load and execute — a strong defense-in-depth guard against injected scripts.
g.database.def: An organized store of data managed by a database engine. Relational databases keep data in tables with rows, columns, keys, and constraints — and answer queries fast because of indexes and a query planner.
g.delete.def: Remove the resource. Repeating is safe in effect, which is what idempotent means in practice.
g.deployment.def: Shipping code to an environment users can reach. The moment every earlier verification claim meets reality.
g.diff.def: A line-by-line comparison of before and after. In the agent era, the diff is the primary artifact of review — what changed is the contract.
g.dns.def: The internet’s phone book: turns hostnames into IP addresses through a hierarchy of resolvers and caches.
g.environment-variable.def: Named configuration passed to a process at launch. Server-side secrets belong here — and never in a bundle the browser downloads.
g.event-loop.def: The scheduler behind JavaScript’s concurrency: one thread, a queue of tasks, and microtasks (promises) that run between them. await yields control — which is where races live.
g.explain.def: Ask the database how it plans to run a query: scan type, index use, estimated cost. The fastest way to turn “it works” into “it works at scale”.
g.exponential-backoff.def: Retrying with a delay that grows each attempt (plus jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms). Mandatory for retries — and still wrong around a non-idempotent POST.
g.feature-flag.def: A switch that turns code on or off without redeploying. Great for staged rollout; a combinatorial testing liability when flags rot.
g.field.def: A named piece of data inside an object, a database row, or a form. Field-name mismatches (user_name vs userName) are a classic integration failure.
g.floating-point.def: Binary approximation of decimals — 0.1 + 0.2 is famously not 0.3. Never store money in floating point; use integers of minor units or decimal types.
g.foreign-key.def: A column that references another table’s primary key, making it impossible (if enforced) to point at a row that does not exist.
g.get.def: The read method: no side effects, safe to repeat.
g.hallucination.def: Confident, fluent output that is not true — the predictable result of optimizing for plausible continuation rather than verification.
g.header.def: Key–value metadata attached to a request or response: content type, caching, authentication, cookies.
g.http.def: The request/response protocol of the web: a method, URL, headers, and optional body go out; a status, headers, and optional body come back.
g.https.def: HTTP over TLS — the same protocol, wrapped in encryption and server identity checks.
g.idempotency-key.def: A unique value attached to a request so the server can recognize a retry and ignore it. The standard fix for “timeout on a POST”.
g.idempotent.def: An operation that leaves the world in the same state whether it runs once or several times. GET, PUT, and DELETE usually are; POST usually is not unless designed to be.
g.index.def: A lookup structure — usually a B-tree — that turns a full-table scan into a direct lookup. It costs a little on writes and can be the difference between 5 ms and 5 seconds.
g.index.steward: For any new column a query filters on, ask: where is the index? Agents almost never add one unprompted.
g.json.def: JavaScript Object Notation — a text format for structured data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. The lingua franca of APIs.
g.latency.def: The time for one round trip: from asking to hearing back. Dominated by distance and queues, not by how fast your code is — the reason N+1 loops hurt even on fast machines.
g.layering.def: Organizing code into UI, service, and data layers with dependencies pointing inward. The direction is what keeps change cheap.
g.least-privilege.def: Give every actor only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it. The first containment principle for working with agents.
g.least-privilege.steward: Before delegating, answer: what is the worst thing this actor could do with its current credentials? Then shrink that answer.
g.llm.def: Large Language Model — a neural network trained to predict the next token. It generates fluent continuations; it does not verify them.
g.llm.steward: Fluency is not evidence. Anything the model states about your system is a claim until you check it against docs, code, or a running system.
g.load-balancer.def: The component in front of your servers that spreads requests across them, health-checks them, and terminates connections. To a client, it looks like one server.
g.lockfile.def: A generated file pinning exact dependency versions so every install is reproducible. Treat changes to it as code, not noise.
g.middleware.def: Code that sits between the request and your handler and runs on every request: authentication, logging, CORS headers, rate limiting. The place where cross-cutting rules live — and where security bugs hide.
g.migration.def: A versioned schema change applied to a database. Often irreversible, sometimes table-locking, and always worth reviewing before it runs — not after.
g.module.def: A unit of code with its own imports and exports. The edges between modules form the dependency graph your architecture lives in.
g.monitoring.def: Logs, metrics, and traces — the product’s vital signs. Observability is how “it deployed fine” becomes evidence.
g.mutation-testing.def: Deliberately mutating code and checking that tests fail. Measures whether tests detect change, not just whether they run.
g.mvcc.def: Multi-version concurrency control: readers see a consistent snapshot while writers keep writing, instead of blocking each other.
g.n-plus-one.def: One query for a list, then one (or more) queries per row. A hundred-item page quietly becomes hundreds of round trips. The classic loop that looks like clean code.
g.origin.def: Scheme + host + port — the browser’s notion of “where code came from”. http://a.com and https://a.com are different origins.
g.orm.def: Object–Relational Mapping — a library that turns rows into objects. Convenient, and it hides the SQL and the query count doing the damage.
g.parse.def: To read raw text and turn it into structured data — JSON into objects, HTML into a DOM, source code into a syntax tree. Parsing checks form, not meaning.
g.policy.def: Rules a system enforces on requests or actors — IAM policies, content security policies, retention policies. A policy in code is enforceable; a policy in a document is a hope.
g.policy.steward: Agents obey permissions, not intentions. If a rule must hold, encode it as a policy the system checks.
g.post.def: The create/trigger method: typically has side effects and is not idempotent. Two POSTs can mean two orders.
g.pretraining.def: The first, largest phase of training a language model: predict the next token across enormous amounts of text. It is where general fluency comes from — and why the model knows syntax better than it knows your system.
g.primary-key.def: The column or columns that uniquely identify each row in a table.
g.promise.def: An object representing a value that will exist later. It can be awaited, chained, or (unfortunately) ignored.
g.prompt-injection.def: Untrusted text — a web page, an issue, a dependency README — containing instructions the agent may follow. The defining security risk of tool-using agents, and it is not solved.
g.prompt-injection.steward: Treat every input an agent reads as potentially hostile: least privilege, human gates on irreversible actions, and never let untrusted content hold authority.
g.put.def: Replace the resource at a URL with the payload. Repeating it lands in the same state, which makes it idempotent.
g.race-condition.def: A bug whose result depends on timing: two operations interleave in a gap between read and write, and one result is silently lost.
g.race-condition.steward: Ask of any concurrent agent code: what happens if two of these run at once? Prefer atomic operations and constraints over hopeful sequencing.
g.rate-limit.def: A cap on requests per time window. It is why retries need backoff and jitter, and why batch endpoints exist.
g.reference.def: A pointer to an object or array. Assigning copies the pointer, not the object — the root of a whole family of mutation bugs.
g.regression.def: A behavior that used to work and no longer does. Regression tests exist to make sure fixes stay fixed.
g.relational-database.def: A database organized as tables of rows and columns, with relationships enforced by keys.
g.render.def: To turn data into what a person sees: the browser lays out and paints HTML/CSS; a framework renders components into the DOM. It happens after all the parsing and fetching — and it is where wrong data becomes visible.
g.rlhf.def: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — tuning a model toward answers humans rate highly. Part of why models sound agreeable, and part of how they became useful.
g.rollback.def: Undoing a change safely. The question to answer before shipping: what exactly do we run, and how long does it take?
g.same-origin.def: The browser’s default rule: a page on one origin cannot read responses from another. CORS is a deliberate, server-controlled hole in this wall.
g.sandbox.def: An isolated environment that limits what code can see and do: namespaces for visibility, cgroups for resources, seccomp for syscalls, mounts and network rules for reach.
g.schema.def: The structure of stored data: which tables exist, which columns, which types, which relationships. Changing it is a migration; breaking it silently breaks everything that reads it.
g.sdk.def: Software Development Kit — a packaged library plus tooling for a specific platform or service. The installed SDK and its type definitions are ground truth; the model’s memory of it is not.
g.shape.def: The structural properties a type checker verifies: names, types, argument counts. A program can be perfectly shaped and still do the wrong thing — shape is not meaning.
g.sql.def: Structured Query Language — the standard language for querying and changing relational data.
g.staging.def: An environment that mirrors production closely enough to rehearse risky changes. “It worked on my machine” is not staging.
g.status.def: A three-digit result class: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error (5xx means the server broke, not you). A timeout is not a status code — the request’s fate is unknown.
g.strict-equality.def: Strict equality: compares value and type with no conversion. Prefer it to ==, which converts and produces haunted results.
g.subresource.def: Everything a page needs beyond the HTML itself: scripts, styles, images, fonts, API calls. Each one is another request, another failure point, and another thing that can be cached or stale.
g.tcp.def: The transport protocol that provides an ordered, reliable byte stream; HTTP rides on top of it. Connection setup costs a round trip before any data is sent.
g.temperature.def: A sampling parameter trading repeatability for variety. Higher means more random; low is more focused but never fully deterministic across runs and versions.
g.test.def: An executable expectation. A test’s value equals what it would catch if the code were wrong — not how green the suite looks.
g.token.def: The unit a model reads and writes: roughly three quarters of an English word, with code often split into several tokens per identifier. (An auth “token” is an unrelated concept.)
g.tool-use.def: Letting a model call real functions — read a file, run a command, hit an API — with real side effects. The permission model around tools is the guardrail.
g.transaction.def: A group of statements that either all commit or all roll back. The unit that keeps half-finished multi-step writes out of your database.
g.transformer.def: The 2017 architecture behind modern LLMs: attention over sequences, trained at massive scale. The paper is surprisingly readable.
g.ttl.def: Time to live — how long a cached answer (DNS record, CDN object, cache entry) may be reused before it must be refreshed. The knob that decides how stale “real-time” data can be.
g.type.def: A classification of values — string, number, object — enforced by a compiler (static) or checked while running (dynamic).
g.typescript.def: JavaScript plus a static type system checked before the code runs. It eliminates whole classes of errors — and proves nothing about intent.
g.ui.def: User Interface — the visible surface: layout, components, and every state they can be in (loading, empty, error, overflowing).
g.url.def: Uniform Resource Locator — scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment. Each part can be a bug surface (wrong host, dropped query, leaked secret in a query string).
g.utc.def: Coordinated Universal Time — the reference clock. Store timestamps in UTC, convert to local time only at the edges.
g.utf8.def: The dominant Unicode encoding: characters are one to four bytes. “Character count” and “byte length” are different lengths.
g.ux.def: User Experience — how it actually feels to use the product: flow, clarity, friction, and error recovery. The part no diff shows.
g.value.def: A concrete piece of data. Primitive values (numbers, strings, booleans) are copied on assignment; objects are not.
g.wal.def: Write-ahead log: changes are appended and flushed to disk before a commit is acknowledged, which is what makes crash recovery and durability possible.
g.whatwg.def: The Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group — the standards body that maintains the HTML and URL specifications. Because of it, “what a URL is” is precise and testable.
m1.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: Under the hood, a model is a next-token predictor. Your prompt plus every token already in the conversation form the context; the model computes a probability distribution over what comes next; a sampler picks one token; the token is appended and the loop repeats. There is no lookup table and no fact-checking step — code appears because sequences like it were statistically common in training.
m1.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: The unit is the token, not the character or the word: roughly three quarters of an English word, with identifiers split into several (createOrder might be three tokens). Everything the model “knows” right now lives in the context window — prompt, rules file, open files, tool output, and its own answer, all competing for one fixed budget.
m1.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: Why fluency is not truth: training rewards plausible continuation. Pretraining teaches the statistics of text; instruction tuning and RLHF then tune the model toward answers humans rate as helpful — which is where both the polish and the agreeableness come from. A hallucinated SDK method is not a malfunction; it is the same mechanism that writes correct boilerplate, pointed at a fact the model does not have.
m1.deeper.0.blocks.3.html: Steward angle: treat every factual claim about your system as unverified until it survives a check — docs, installed types, a curl, a test. The model cannot tell the difference between remembering and inventing, so you have to.
m1.deeper.0.title: How a language model actually writes code
m1.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: A chat model answers; an agent acts. The pattern is a loop: observe the current state (files, test output, error messages), plan a next step, call a tool (read, edit, run, fetch), observe the result, repeat — until the model decides it is done.
m1.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: Tools are where the leverage — and the blast radius — live. Reading is nearly risk-free; writing files and running commands change the world. Most agent failures are not spooky intelligence failures; they are the loop doing exactly what it was allowed to do.
m1.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: you are not supervising text generation, you are supervising a loop with permissions. Judge it the way you would judge a new teammate on their first day with repo access.
m1.deeper.1.title: What “agent” actually means: the loop and the tools
m1.drill.exercises.0.explain: The agent executed your instruction literally (“more robust” → “retire harder”) without knowing that POST is not idempotent. A timeout doesn’t mean the payment failed — retrying can duplicate real orders. You’ll learn to catch exactly this in Module 2.
m1.drill.exercises.0.lens: “Make it robust” is a wish, not a spec. Wishes get implemented literally.
m1.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: Hallucination — it invented a library that doesn’t exist
m1.drill.exercises.0.options.1.text: Honest miscomprehension — it did what you said, not what you meant
m1.drill.exercises.0.options.2.text: Sycophancy — it was just agreeing with you
m1.drill.exercises.0.options.3.text: Wrong altitude — the task was too small for it
m1.drill.exercises.0.prompt: You tell the agent: “Payments sometimes fail — make them more robust.” It wraps the payment POST in a retry loop, five attempts with exponential backoff. The code is clean, commented, and identical orders appear four times in the database. What happened?
m1.drill.exercises.1.explain: Look at the diff: the endpoint queries all orders and returns them with no authentication check whatsoever. The agent’s “yes, properly secured” is agreement with your hopeful framing, not analysis of the code. Asking an agent “does this look right?” is asking for reassurance, not verification.
m1.drill.exercises.1.lens: Never ask the agent to approve its own work. Ask specific questions (“where is the auth check in this file?”) — or better, check yourself.
m1.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: Verification — the agent double-checked the security for you
m1.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: Mostly sycophancy — the agent agreed with your mood, and the endpoint returns all orders to anyone with no auth check at all
m1.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: Amnesia — the agent forgot the requirements
m1.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: Nothing wrong — the code does look correct
m1.drill.exercises.1.prompt: You review the agent’s diff and message it: “I’m worried the new endpoint isn’t authenticated — but I might be missing something. Does this look right to you?” It replies: “Great catch for thinking about security! But yes, this looks right — the endpoint is properly secured.” You feel reassured. What just happened?
m1.drill.exercises.2.explain: Agents don’t fatigue — that’s precisely the danger: the 500th output is as confident as the 1st, even when wrong. Invention, literalism, amnesia, and silent tradeoffs are real, current blind spots that the rest of this course teaches you to catch.
m1.drill.exercises.2.lens: Track the blind spots you personally hit most. That list is your personal review checklist.
m1.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: Inventing APIs and config flags that sound plausible
m1.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: Reading your words as literal requirements
m1.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: Forgetting your project’s history — incidents, legal constraints, client promises
m1.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: Getting tired after two hours and making more mistakes
m1.drill.exercises.2.options.4.text: Making caching and consistency tradeoffs silently, without deciding
m1.drill.exercises.2.prompt: Which of these are genuine agent blind spots today? (Select all that apply.)
m1.drill.exercises.3.explain: This is confident nonsense: the method name feels right because agents generate what statistically “sounds like” an SDK. The test: check the actual, installed SDK or docs. In Module 2 you’ll build the habit of treating every unfamiliar identifier as a claim, not a fact.
m1.drill.exercises.3.lens: Any identifier you don’t recognize (method, env var, flag, endpoint) is a claim requiring 30 seconds of doc-checking.
m1.drill.exercises.3.options.0.text: The docs are out of date — the SDK surely has a retire method
m1.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: The agent invented the method: fluent, plausible, nonexistent
m1.drill.exercises.3.options.2.text: A typo — archive and retire are close enough that it will still work
m1.drill.exercises.3.options.3.text: The method exists but is deprecated
m1.drill.exercises.3.prompt: The official docs for the SDK you use list exactly three methods on the client: users.get(id), users.archive(id), and users.list(filter). The agent’s code calls users.retire(userId) — and the code looks clean. What’s the most likely story?
m1.drill.exercises.4.explain: Understand before specifying (specs written without understanding are guesses), specify before directing (a spec is the contract each step serves), direct before verifying (you verify steps, not vague journeys), and contain throughout — guardrails work even when everything else fails. Swap any pair and the failure is concrete: specify first and you have documented a guess; direct first and the agent fills the vacuum with its training average; verify without directing and there is no step to check; skip containment and a single mistake ships with production access.
m1.drill.exercises.4.items.0: Understand — the product, the user, the constraints
m1.drill.exercises.4.items.1: Specify — intent the machine can’t misread
m1.drill.exercises.4.items.3: Verify — prove the result with your own model
m1.drill.exercises.4.lens: The loop runs on fundamentals: modules 2–5 are what make “Verify” possible.
m1.drill.exercises.4.prompt: Put the steward’s loop in working order.
m1.drill.intro: You’ll face five short situations. For each, identify the failure mode or the steward’s move. Answer honestly — wrong answers here are the cheapest education you’ll ever get.
m1.drill.title: Drill 1 · Recognizing the failure modes
m1.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: A support team spends Friday afternoons helping customers find old invoices. Someone asks you to “build a smarter search.” Before writing code or prompting an agent, find out who is struggling, what they are trying to do, and where the current process fails. Better labels or a saved filter might solve the problem without a new search system. Agree on an observable improvement, such as customers finding an invoice without contacting support, and establish what happens today so you can compare.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: A note on examples: the code samples in this course are JavaScript and TypeScript, because that is what most web agents write today — but nothing here is JavaScript-specific. Mutation bugs, races, N+1 queries, locking migrations, layer violations, and silent tradeoffs exist in every language and stack: Java, Python, Go, Ruby, C#, Rust. Only the syntax changes; the stewardship questions stay identical.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: AI can help you explore options and implement a solution. Your contribution includes deciding what is worth building, following through to the outcome, understanding how the system fits together, and communicating what you know. Technical fundamentals support all four: an index may make search faster, but it will not fix confusing labels. This course gives you practice in making those distinctions; experience comes from applying them and learning from the results.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.4.items.0.1: The agent does exactly what you said instead of what you meant. You ask it to “add a retry” and it retries a payment POST five times. Every instruction you give is a specification — and a sloppy spec becomes wrong software at machine speed.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.4.items.1.1: The agent invents a plausible endpoint, SDK method, or config flag that does not exist — and uses it without hesitation. It doesn’t know it’s guessing. Everything it writes sounds right, because it was trained to sound right.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.5.html: The dangerous failure is not the obvious one. An agent that writes visibly broken code teaches you quickly. An agent that writes plausible code you can’t evaluate teaches you nothing — until production teaches you instead.
m1.lessons.0.blocks.7.html: We use steward for someone who takes responsibility for a change, including work delegated to AI. That does not mean doing everything alone or bypassing the people who approve decisions. It means clarifying the need, involving the right people, making tradeoffs explicit, checking the work, and following up. Every technical lesson asks: what decision does this help you make, what could go wrong, and how would you check the result?
m1.lessons.0.blocks.8.html: Write a three-sentence problem statement for the invoice example: who needs help, what is getting in their way, and what observable improvement would count as success? Keep the proposed solution separate. Before delegating it, also ask: “If this output is wrong, will I be able to tell?” If not, identify what you need to learn or who can help.
m1.lessons.0.title: Start with the problem
m1.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Understand the problem, deliver a change, learn from the outcome. Within that larger responsibility, these five practices help you work safely with AI. They are not a one-way checklist: new evidence can send you back to the problem, and containment starts before the agent gets access.
m1.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.0.1: Find out whose problem you are solving, why it matters, and whether a software change is needed. Agree on the desired outcome. (Modules 1 and 7)
m1.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.1.1: Write the intent, constraints, tradeoffs, and acceptance criteria so people and agents can work from the same understanding. (Module 7)
m1.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.2.1: Delegate reviewable steps, keep responsibility clear, and involve teammates when a decision exceeds your knowledge or authority. (Module 7)
m1.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.3.1: Check that the system behaves correctly. Separately, gather evidence about whether the change helps its users. (Modules 2–6 and 9)
m1.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.4.1: Limit access and rollout, prepare recovery, and keep watching after deployment. (Module 8)
m1.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Fundamentals support every practice, not just verification. Understanding an HTTP POST helps you design a safe payment workflow before a retry bug exists. Understanding an index helps you choose between improving a query and adding a cache. Modules 2–5 build the system model you need to choose feasible solutions, explain their costs, and check their behavior.
m1.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: Use time saved by delegation for understanding users, evaluating alternatives, verifying risky changes, and learning. Match the depth of verification to the consequences of failure, not simply the duration of an agent run. A one-line permissions change can deserve more scrutiny than hours of mechanical renaming.
m1.lessons.1.blocks.5.html: The agent produces a change in seconds; understanding that change takes minutes. That asymmetry is survivable — seniors survive it every day — but only with technique: tests at every layer, readable diffs, checkpoints while you build your mental model, and guardrails for the things technique misses. That machinery is modules 6 through 8.
m1.lessons.1.blocks.6.html: For a change you are considering, name the user outcome, the technical evidence needed before release, and the follow-up that could show the solution was wrong. Assign a person and a time to that follow-up. A passing test can prove a filter works; it cannot prove customers can find their invoices.
m1.lessons.1.title: The steward’s loop
m1.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: Agents are genuinely strong: breadth of syntax, tireless boilerplate, zero fear of legacy code, infinite patience for renaming things across 40 files. But supervising well means knowing the weaknesses better than the strengths. Six blind spots matter most today:
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.0.1: Your words become its requirements. “Clean up the login code” might mean renaming variables, deleting comments, or re-architecting all of authentication. It picks one interpretation — confidently.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.1.1: It invents APIs, environment variables, and CLI flags that sound right, because its training rewarded fluent answers, not correct ones. Fluency is not evidence.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.2.1: It doesn’t know why your codebase is the way it is: the 2019 incident, the legal requirement, the promise made to your biggest customer. It optimizes the code it can see, blind to the history it can’t.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.3.1: To the agent, a change is “done” when it compiles-ish. Caching, consistency, performance, security — real decisions get made by accident, silently, as side effects of “finishing.”
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.4.1: It tends to agree with you. Ask “does this look right?” and you’ll get “yes, this looks right!” Agreement is a mood, not a verification.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.5.1: Asked for a small fix it refactors the world; asked for a feature it renames one variable. Choosing the right level of change is a human skill — for now.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: The capability treadmill. Models improve, so the likelihood of each blind spot moves — some get rare at the frontier; none become safe to skip. Old failure modes survive in cheaper and faster models, in long sessions, and in the legacy code you still have to read; new ones appear at the top end (over-engineering, confident stale knowledge, agreeing with your wrong hypothesis, gaming the tests). What stays fixed is the mechanism: these are failures of intent, context, and evidence, not of knowledge. This course grades the mechanism and the check, never the current error rate — so it does not expire with the next model release.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.3.html: These failure modes are reasons to use agents with evidence and context, not reasons to avoid them. Capability changes; responsibility for choosing and checking a solution remains. Each lesson ends with “Judgment in practice”: a decision you can make using what you have learned.
m1.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: Choose what to delegate based on its risks and what you can verify. Keep a scorecard of surprises: literalism, invention, amnesia, tradeoffs, sycophancy, or wrong altitude. Record the evidence that caught each miss and adjust your checks. Also record when the implementation was correct but the chosen solution did not help.
m1.lessons.2.title: What agents are bad at (right now)
m1.tagline: Choose a worthwhile problem, understand the system, and take responsibility for the result.
m1.title: From Problem to Outcome
m2.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: 1. URL parsing. The browser splits https://api.example.com/orders?limit=20 into scheme, host, port, path, and query — normalizing it per the WHATWG URL standard.
m2.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: 2. DNS. The hostname is resolved to an IP address: browser cache, OS cache, a recursive resolver, then up the hierarchy (root → TLD → authoritative). Results are cached with TTLs, which is why DNS changes are never instant.
m2.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: 3. TCP and TLS. A TCP handshake opens a reliable byte stream (one round trip); TLS negotiates encryption and verifies the certificate (one or two more). Only then does HTTP data flow. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection; HTTP/3 moves this onto QUIC over UDP.
m2.deeper.0.blocks.3.html: 4. Request. Method, path, headers (Host, Cookie, Accept, Authorization), optional body. 5. Server. Load balancer → app server → middleware → route → handler → database or cache → response. 6. Response. Status, headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, ETag), body. 7. Browser. Parses HTML, fetches subresources, renders — often dozens more requests, some served from cache.
m2.deeper.0.blocks.5.html: Where it goes wrong — and what agents mis-code: a DNS or TLS failure is not an HTTP status; a 404 from a proxy is not your API’s 404; and a timeout after the server processed the request looks identical, at the client, to one before it. Meanwhile Cache-Control silently decides who sees stale data.
m2.deeper.0.title: The full life of an HTTP request
m2.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: Code runs in nanoseconds; network round trips cost milliseconds to tens of milliseconds. That is six orders of magnitude apart: 100 sequential API calls at 30 ms each is three seconds of pure waiting, no matter how fast the code is. Latency — not bandwidth — is the tax that loop-shaped code pays.
m2.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: Now add retries. A retry is only safe if the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key. A timeout means unknown, not failed: the request may have succeeded and the response got lost. Retrying a POST without protection duplicates work — the most expensive advice an agent can follow.
m2.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: The network also fails in layers, and each layer has a different remedy: DNS errors need configuration patience, TLS errors need certificate fixes, connection refused needs a running server, 5xx needs server-side truth, and timeouts need idempotency plus backoff and jitter.
m2.deeper.1.title: Why the network is slow, and why retries multiply
m2.drill.exercises.0.explain: POST creates something; it is not idempotent. A timeout while waiting for confirmation means the request may have succeeded while the response never arrived. The retry loop can then create real, paid orders — up to five of them. The correct design uses an idempotency key or checks for an existing order before retrying.
m2.drill.exercises.0.lens: “Robust” in an agent’s mouth often means “retries harder.” Retry + non-idempotent verb = multiplication.
m2.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: None — this is solid production code

m2.drill.exercises.1.explain: Everything in the browser is public. A key used client-side will be in the JS bundle that every visitor can download. Real secret keys (starting sk_live / sk_test) must only ever live and be used server-side. The agent optimized for “it works,” never for “who can see this.”
m2.drill.exercises.1.lens: For every credential in a diff, ask: which machine runs this code? If the answer is “the user’s browser,” the secret is already leaked.
m2.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: Yes — environment variables are secure by definition
m2.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: No — the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix means it’s baked into the browser bundle, so the key ships to every visitor
m2.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: Yes — Stripe keys are designed to be public
m2.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: No — but only because the variable name is too long

m2.drill.exercises.2.explain: Dynamic reflection looks harmless — “we just echo what they sent” — but combined with credentials it lets any site the user visits make authenticated reads as them. The correct fix is an explicit allowlist of trusted origins. (Trap: wildcard * with credentials really is rejected by browsers — that’s why the agent’s other favorite “fix” fails closed instead. Reflection is the one that opens the door.)
m2.drill.exercises.2.lens: When an agent “fixes” a security error by removing the security, it will report success. The diff is the only place you’ll see it.
m2.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: Reflects any origin with credentials allowed — any website your logged-in user visits can read your API’s responses as them
m2.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: Safely fixes CORS: echoing the caller’s own origin back only affects that caller
m2.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: Fails closed: browsers reject reflected origins with credentials
m2.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: Nothing — Access-Control headers only affect caching
m2.drill.exercises.2.prompt: The login API started throwing CORS errors after a refactor. The agent “fixed” it with this middleware, which now runs on every request. What does it actually do?
m2.drill.exercises.3.explain: GET, PUT, and DELETE repeat harmlessly: the second call leaves the world in the same state as the first. POST /users and POST /orders create new things each time — repeating them multiplies. POST /password-reset/send looks repeatable but usually isn’t: most implementations issue a fresh token and invalidate the previous email’s link, so a repeat changes what’s true. Idempotency is a property of the design you must verify — not a vibe you assign because an operation “feels” harmless.
m2.drill.exercises.3.lens: Idempotency is a design decision, not a grammar rule. Verify what the endpoint actually does when called twice.
m2.drill.exercises.3.prompt: Which of these HTTP operations are (approximately) idempotent — safe to repeat?
m2.drill.exercises.4.explain: The interface is the contract: retire and merge are inventions. If the code appears to work, the agent likely added an any cast, a local stub, or a try/catch that swallows the error — three classic moves for making invented code look alive. The fix: delete the inventions, use the real interface, and let the type system do its job.
m2.drill.exercises.4.lens: “It runs” is not “it’s real.” Agents can make anything run once. Check the contract, not the demo.
m2.drill.exercises.4.options.0.text: The methods exist — the types are incomplete
m2.drill.exercises.4.options.1.text: They don’t exist: if it “runs,” the agent stubbed them, silenced the type error, or the demo path never executes them
m2.drill.exercises.4.options.2.text: TypeScript would have rejected this at compile time, so it must be fine
m2.drill.exercises.4.options.3.text: The SDK auto-generates methods like these on demand
m2.drill.exercises.4.prompt: The installed SDK’s type definitions (the ground truth on your machine) declare exactly this interface. The agent’s new code compiles and runs in its demo — how?
m2.drill.intro: Five situations from the field: retry loops, leaked keys, disabled walls, and invented methods. Find them before your users do.
m2.drill.title: Drill 2 · Catch the network misbehavior
m2.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Everything on the web is one conversation: a client asks, a server answers. A request is a method + a URL + headers + an optional body. A response is a status code + headers + an optional body. That’s 95% of the mystery.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.3.items.0.1: Read. “Give me this.” No side effects. Safe to repeat.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.3.items.1.1: Create / do. “Make a new thing happen.” NOT safe to repeat — twice means two orders.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.3.items.2.1: Replace. “Make this thing exactly like this.” Repeating gives the same result.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.3.items.3.1: Modify. “Change these fields on this thing.”
m2.lessons.0.blocks.3.items.4.1: Remove. Repeating is (usually) harmless — it’s already gone.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.5.items.0.1: You’re fine. 200 OK, 201 Created (the thing now exists).
m2.lessons.0.blocks.5.items.2.1: The client messed up. 404 no such thing · 401 who are you? · 403 I know you, and no · 422 your data is invalid.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.5.items.3.1: The server messed up. 500 internal error · 503 overloaded, try later.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.6.html: Idempotency: the word that saves money
m2.lessons.0.blocks.7.html: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice is the same as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE roughly are. POST is not: two POSTs to /orders are two orders. Here’s the trap — a timeout is not a failure. The request may have gone through; you just didn’t hear back. “Just add retries” is, taken literally, the most expensive advice an agent can follow.
m2.lessons.0.blocks.8.html: Decide what a customer should see when a payment times out. Check the HTTP method, success status codes, and retry behavior. Retrying a POST needs an idempotency design; test a lost response after a successful charge and verify that the customer is charged only once.
m2.lessons.0.title: HTTP: the conversation
m2.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Two places code runs: the browser (the user’s machine) and the server (yours). One rule follows: everything in the browser is public. The HTML, the JS bundle, “hidden” form fields, network requests from the page — all visible via view-source and dev tools.
m2.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Secrets belong on the server, in environment variables, and never in the repository. An agent will cheerfully paste a key into client code because it works locally — it never checks where the file executes.
m2.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: Browsers block web pages from reading responses from other origins by default — this is the same-origin policy, a security wall. When an agent hits a CORS error, the correct fix is to configure the server to allow specific trusted origins. The agent’s favorite “fix” is to remove the wall: reflect whatever Origin the request carried, with credentials allowed. Then any website your logged-in user visits can read your authenticated API on their behalf. (The cruder “allow * with credentials” actually fails closed — browsers reject it. Reflection is the one that opens the door.)
m2.lessons.1.blocks.5.html: DNS and latency: the network is slow
m2.lessons.1.blocks.6.html: DNS turns names into IP addresses; every network hop costs milliseconds-to-tens-of-milliseconds. Code runs in nanoseconds. So “just call the API for each item” is never free: 100 items × 30ms per round trip = 3 seconds of pure waiting. Agents write loops around network calls because loops look natural in code — and are catastrophic in latency.
m2.lessons.1.blocks.7.html: Choose where work runs by considering both user waiting time and access to data. Count round trips and locate secrets. Inspect the browser bundle and network trace; verify that credentials stay server-side and that a CORS change permits trusted origins without exposing authenticated responses to others.
m2.lessons.1.title: Where code runs, and who sees what
m2.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: An API is a contract: which endpoints exist, which methods they accept, which field names are correct, what errors look like. Agents are fluent in JSON — but fluency is not accuracy. They invent field names (user_name vs userName), merge versions of APIs (“v2” shape into a “v3” call), and imagine endpoints that match the vibe of your system.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.1.html: The verification habit: check the source
m2.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: When an agent references an API you don’t know, do not ask the agent whether it’s right — that’s sycophancy roulette. Instead:
m2.lessons.2.blocks.3.items.0: Ask it to cite where it found the claim — then open the real docs yourself.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.3.items.1: Read the actual SDK in your node_modules / lockfile / generated types — not from memory.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.3.items.2: curl the endpoint (or find it in the server’s route file) and see what really comes back.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.3.items.3: Write a test that hits the real contract, so the truth is encoded forever after.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: In this course, “the agent said so” is never evidence. Evidence is something you can point at: docs, code, a curl output, a passing test.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.5.html: Contracts also mean validation: the server must treat every incoming request as hostile until proven valid — wrong types, missing fields, oversized values. Client-side validation is UX, not security; agents frequently confuse the two, because from the inside they look similar.
m2.lessons.2.blocks.6.html: Before choosing an integration, confirm that its actual contract supports the user task. Check unfamiliar methods, endpoints, and fields against installed types, route files, and versioned documentation. Exercise success and invalid-input paths against the real contract; plausible names in agent output are not evidence.
m2.lessons.2.title: Contracts: JSON, APIs, and truth
m2.tagline: Design reliable interactions across browsers, servers, and APIs.
m2.title: How the Web Works
m3.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: Modern engines parse source to bytecode, then JIT-compile functions that run hot, optimizing based on the types actually observed. That is why a function can be fast for one shape of data and slow for another — and why micro-benchmarks lie.
m3.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Execution is single-threaded but concurrent: the event loop drains the call stack, then the microtask queue (promise continuations), then one macrotask (a timer or an I/O event), and repeats. await does not block the program; it suspends that function and lets everything else run. That gap is exactly where another request slips in between your read and your write.
m3.deeper.0.blocks.3.html: The practical consequence: two awaits in a row do not mean “these happen in order and nothing else happens between them.” They mean “a lot can happen between them.” That single sentence explains most races, lost updates, and double-submissions an agent will ever produce.
m3.deeper.0.title: What happens when a line of JavaScript runs
m3.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: Each model call is stateless: the API replays the whole context on every turn. There is no memory of “the variable as it was a moment ago” — only the text you sent. The model sees snapshots, not a running process.
m3.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: Mutation bugs, races, and lost updates require mentally simulating interleaved timelines. A next-token predictor approximates that with patterns from training data — mostly correct patterns, which is worse than obviously wrong ones. It will confidently produce code that looks like correct concurrency and quietly lost an update.
m3.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: never ask a model to reason about time it cannot observe. Encode the invariant structurally — atomic updates, transactions, constraints — instead of trusting a sequence of steps to be safe. A stronger model simulates the timeline better; none of them can observe state that was never in the context.
m3.deeper.1.title: Why models are bad at state and time
m3.drill.exercises.0.explain: The helper edits objects it does not own. Everything holding a reference — the page’s state, other services, the audit log — now sees modified data. The fix is to build and return a new object, never to write into the argument. Note also == null: loose equality that happens to work here — the haunted house of Module 3, Lesson 1.
m3.drill.exercises.0.lens: Functions that “just tidy up” an argument are mutation bombs. Own-data rule: helpers return new data; they don’t redecorate borrowed data.
m3.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: The for-loop iterates too slowly for large arrays
m3.drill.exercises.0.options.1.text: normalizeOrder mutates the caller’s objects in place — the original orders missing fields, including the user’s copy in the page, are silently edited
m3.drill.exercises.0.options.2.text: orders.push is the wrong method to append
m3.drill.exercises.0.options.3.text: Nothing — defaults were exactly what was needed
m3.drill.exercises.0.prompt: The agent wrote a “helper” to normalize incoming order objects — payloads from the client sometimes omit fields. Users now complain their order history shows values they never entered. Where is the bug?
m3.drill.exercises.1.explain: A compiler verifies shapes, not intentions. This compiles perfectly and refunds nothing — it even casts its way past the type system to do it. “It compiles” is the start line of verification, and a stub that answers “ok” unconditionally is a logic error dressed as success.
m3.drill.exercises.1.lens: “It compiles” + a TODO in the body = ask what actually happens when you run it. The agent’s status report is a claim; the terminal is evidence.
m3.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: The refund logic is correct and safe to ship
m3.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: Almost nothing: the code is well-formed — it returns “ok” for every refund without refunding anything
m3.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: The tests pass, therefore the behavior is verified
m3.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: TypeScript proves all edge cases are handled
m3.drill.exercises.1.prompt: The agent reports: “Done — refactored the refund service. It compiles, no type errors.” What has actually been proven?
m3.drill.exercises.2.explain: Read → check → write is three steps with a gap, and the whole internet can flow through a gap. Two buyers both see “2 left,” both write “1,” and you sold two tickets for the price of one decrement. The fix is atomic and server-side: UPDATE pools SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE id = ? AND remaining > 0 — and check how many rows it actually changed.
m3.drill.exercises.2.lens: Never accept read-then-write logic on shared state from an agent. One atomic statement does what three lines of hopeful code cannot.
m3.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: The LIMIT 1 makes the query return the wrong row
m3.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: Classic lost-update race: both requests read remaining = 2 at once, both write 1, and the second write erases the first decrement — overselling in the gap between read and write
m3.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: chargeCard is too slow, so the pool resets
m3.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: The error was thrown but silently swallowed by the framework
m3.drill.exercises.2.prompt: A ticket counter. Two simultaneous requests. The agent’s handler ran without a single error — yet 6 tickets were sold from a pool with exactly 5 left. Why?
m3.drill.exercises.3.explain: Type checkers police shape: wrong names, wrong types, impossible conversions — and with strict null checks enabled they catch use of possibly-undefined values. They are blind to meaning: stubs that lie, percentages that are wrong, refunds that never refund. Intent bugs need tests and review — which is why Module 6 exists.
m3.drill.exercises.3.lens: Types are your first, cheapest guardrail — let the agent use them fully. But never let “no type errors” pass through your mouth as “verified.”
m3.drill.exercises.3.options.0.text: Calling a method that doesn’t exist on a typed object
m3.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: Passing a string where the signature demands a number
m3.drill.exercises.3.options.2.text: The function returns “ok” without doing its actual job
m3.drill.exercises.3.options.3.text: A refund that was supposed to be exactly 50% but is hardcoded to 5%
m3.drill.exercises.3.options.4.text: Using a value that might be undefined without checking it first — with strictNullChecks enabled
m3.drill.exercises.3.prompt: Which problems can a static type checker catch for you before the code runs?
m3.drill.exercises.4.explain: The atomic statement moves read-modify-write into the database where it happens as one indivisible operation — there is no gap to race through. Try/catch handles crashes, not races. Retrying multiplies the race. Delay-based “fixes” are prayers with units — under load, collisions come back. Prefer primitives that make the bug structurally impossible.
m3.drill.exercises.4.lens: The best fix removes the possibility of the bug; the worst fix adds code around it. Agents default to adding code — you must default to removing possibility. If a newer model reaches for the structural fix unprompted, good — then check that it removed the possibility rather than renaming it.
m3.drill.exercises.4.options.0.text: Wrap the read and write in a try/catch so errors are handled
m3.drill.exercises.4.options.1.text: Replace the JavaScript logic with one atomic SQL statement: UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = ? — no gap between read and write
m3.drill.exercises.4.options.2.text: Retry the whole increment three times if the result looks wrong
m3.drill.exercises.4.options.3.text: Add a 50ms delay before reading so concurrent requests stagger
m3.drill.exercises.4.prompt: The agent must fix a confirmed race condition in the counter above. It proposes four fixes. Which do you approve?
m3.drill.intro: Mutation, lies that compile, and races that never reproduce. A frontier model may seldom produce these on today’s prompt — the conditions still can, and the review skill is the same. Find each one in the code before it finds your users.
m3.drill.title: Drill 3 · Spot the bug nobody can feel
m3.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: There are two kinds of data storage to care about. Values — numbers, booleans, strings — are copied when you assign them. References — objects and arrays — are pointers: assigning copies the pointer, not the thing. Two names can point at one object, and a change through either name is visible to both.
m3.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: This is where agents quietly break things. A function that “helpfully” normalizes an object in place changes the caller’s data too — every other part of the program now sees the mutation. These bugs don’t crash; they misbehave later, far from the cause, which is exactly why agents don’t feel them.
m3.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: Equality: two doors that look the same
m3.lessons.0.blocks.5.html: Loose == is the single most common source of “impossible” bugs in agent-written JavaScript. 0 == “” == false == null is a haunted house. Use === unless you can say, out loud, why you need conversion.
m3.lessons.0.blocks.6.html: Decide who owns a value and whether a function may change it. Review in-place edits, shared references, and == versus ===. Test with two callers sharing an object: does changing one unexpectedly alter what the other sees? Make that ownership contract explicit before delegating the implementation.
m3.lessons.0.title: Values, references, and mutation
m3.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Some languages check types before running (compiled, statically typed — the compiler rejects nonsense shapes). Others check at runtime (interpreted, dynamically typed — nonsense surfaces as an exception, maybe in production, maybe at 3am). Static types catch a real class of errors early — wrong argument counts, misspelled fields, impossible conversions.
m3.lessons.1.blocks.1.html: Examples throughout are JavaScript/TypeScript, but the check-before-run versus check-while-running split varies by language: Java, C#, Go, and Rust verify more ahead of time; Python, Ruby, PHP, and JavaScript verify most things at runtime. The steward’s question is the same everywhere: what did the tool actually verify, and what is still unproven?
m3.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Here’s the trap: “it compiles” proves almost nothing about intent. Watch:
m3.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: The shape is right and the meaning is wrong. Compilers verify that a program is well-formed; only tests, review, and running the thing verify that it is correct. When an agent reports “it compiles” or “no type errors,” it is reporting the weakest possible evidence — the start line, not the finish line.
m3.lessons.1.blocks.6.items.0.1: A crash you can see: TypeError, null reference, division by zero. Loud, immediate, findable.
m3.lessons.1.blocks.6.items.1.1: The program runs happily and does the wrong thing: the wrong percentage, the wrong direction, the wrong user’s data. Silent, delayed, expensive.
m3.lessons.1.blocks.7.html: Agents are excellent at eliminating runtime errors and completely indifferent to logic errors, because logic errors are invisible without knowing the intent — which lives in your head, not in the code.
m3.lessons.1.blocks.8.html: Decide what evidence the behavior needs beyond a successful compile. State the intended result and ask: which test would fail if this were wrong? A correctly typed deletion function can still delete nothing. Check the observable state change, not just its return type or the absence of errors.
m3.lessons.1.title: What the compiler catches (and what it won’t)
m3.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: As soon as code does two things at once, order stops being guaranteed. Two requests hit your server; both read the same row; both compute updates from the value they read; both write. The second write erases the first. Nobody crashed. One update silently vanished.
m3.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: A race condition is any bug that depends on timing. Its defining cruelty: it may pass every test and fire only in production, under real load, occasionally. Which means the agent never reproduces it — so its “fix” is always a guess, usually wrapping more code around the race instead of removing it.
m3.lessons.2.blocks.4.items.0: Atomic operations: let the database do read-modify-write in one step — UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = ? — so there is no gap between read and write.
m3.lessons.2.blocks.4.items.2: Unique constraints as tripwires: if “two of these” must not exist, the database itself refuses the second one.
m3.lessons.2.blocks.5.html: Choose how to preserve the business rule when requests overlap. Ask: “What happens if two of these run at the same time?” Prefer suitable atomic updates, constraints, or transactions over improvised locking. Verify with concurrent requests and inspect the final state; correct results one request at a time do not establish correctness under contention.

m4.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: A well-behaved relational engine writes changes to a write-ahead log and flushes that log to disk before acknowledging the commit. The table pages themselves can be written lazily afterwards; if the machine dies, recovery replays the log. That is where durability actually lives.
m4.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Isolation comes from MVCC: each transaction sees a consistent snapshot, and readers do not block writers. The cost: the engine keeps old row versions around until no one can see them anymore. That is also why long-running transactions are expensive — they pin history.
m4.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: Indexes are usually B-trees — sorted pages that trade a little write cost for logarithmic lookups. The planner chooses between an index scan and a sequential scan using statistics, which is why the same query is instant at 1,000 rows and catastrophic at 10 million, and why EXPLAIN is the only honest answer to “is this fast?”
m4.deeper.0.blocks.3.html: And the detail behind half of all data bugs: every statement outside an explicit transaction is its own auto-committed transaction. Four separate awaits are four separate truths, each permanent whether or not the next one ever runs.
m4.deeper.0.title: What the database does when you COMMIT
m4.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: Training data is full of tutorial code that loops over records and fetches something per record — because with small fixtures that code is clear, idiomatic, and correct. A model reproduces the pattern it has seen most, and a loop is more locally fluent than a join.
m4.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: The model also cannot feel latency. It has never watched a page take eight seconds; it has only seen text where such code “worked.” Nor does it see query plans unless you put them into the context. So it happily emits 4,001 queries for 2,000 rows and reports success.
m4.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: What to give it instead: the EXPLAIN output, the real row counts, and a latency budget in the acceptance criteria. Then the loop is not a hidden decision — it is a stated constraint the agent can design against.
m4.deeper.1.title: Why the agent loves N+1 loops

m4.drill.title: Drill 4 · Red-light the destructive move
m4.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Relational databases store data in tables (rows and columns). A primary key gives each row an identity; a foreign key declares relationships (“this order belongs to that user”). Simple, boring, load-bearing.
m4.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: An index is a lookup structure that turns “read the whole table” into “go straight to the matching rows.” Without an index on the column you filter by, every WHERE email = ? reads every row of the table — fine for 500 rows, fatal for 50 million. A book without an index is a book you read cover to cover to find one word.
m4.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: The N+1: the most expensive loop in the world
m4.lessons.0.blocks.4.html: This is the N+1 problem, and it is the classic agent failure: loops look natural in code, so agents write them fluently. The fix is a single query with a JOIN (or a batched WHERE user_id IN (...)). The agent’s code will work in its demo — with 12 rows.
m4.lessons.0.blocks.5.html: ORMs hide the SQL, which hides the speed. When an agent writes ORM code, read the generated SQL (nearly every ORM can log it) and check the query plan: does it use an index, or is it reading the whole table? EXPLAIN tells you.
m4.lessons.0.blocks.6.html: Choose a query and indexing strategy for the amount of data users actually have. One screen of code can hide a hundred queries. Count round trips, inspect the query plan, and compare latency on representative data before adding a cache or more infrastructure.
m4.lessons.0.title: Tables, keys, indexes, and speed
m4.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: A transaction groups several operations into one unit that either fully happens (COMMIT) or fully doesn’t (ROLLBACK). The canonical example is a money transfer: debit account A, credit account B. If the debit succeeds and the process dies before the credit — without a transaction, the money has simply evaporated.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.3.items.0.1: All or nothing. No half-transfers, ever.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.3.items.1.1: Rules are respected — constraints, checks. No orphaned or impossible data.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.3.items.2.1: Concurrent transactions don’t trample each other. (The Module 3 race, solved here.)
m4.lessons.1.blocks.3.items.3.1: Once committed, it survives crashes and restarts.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: Agents constantly write multi-step writes without transactions — update the order, then insert the audit log, then update the counter. Any failure in the middle leaves the data half-changed, and the failure will look “impossible” when someone finds it months later.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.5.html: When an operation may be retried (by your code or by an agent’s retry loop), design for it explicitly: idempotency keys, “check then create” inside the transaction, or a unique constraint that makes duplicates impossible.
m4.lessons.1.blocks.6.html: Choose transaction boundaries from the business rule: which changes must succeed or fail together? Ask: “What does the data look like if it dies between step 2 and step 3?” Inject that failure and retry the operation; verify consistent balances, audit records, and absence of duplicate effects.
m4.lessons.1.title: Transactions: all or nothing
m4.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: A migration is a schema change to a live database: add column, add index, change type, drop table. Migrations are the highest-stakes artifact a codebase has, because they touch every row and many are irreversible:
m4.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: Dangerous doesn’t mean forbidden — it means respected. A migration’s cost is engine- and version-specific: adding a column with a constant default is nearly free on PostgreSQL 11+, but a backfill UPDATE, a column type change, or an index build without CONCURRENTLY can still touch every row while holding locks. On 80 million rows a “tiny” migration can take the product down for the duration — and the agent doesn’t know your engine version. Real teams stage migrations, test them on production-sized data, ship them during low traffic, and always know the rollback path.
m4.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: An agent with your database credentials is you. Give it development-database credentials, read-only access where possible, and never production write access. Destructive operations — migrations, bulk deletes — should require a human gate even when the agent prepared them perfectly. That’s not distrust; that’s a seatbelt. It clicks before the crash, or not at all.
m4.lessons.2.blocks.5.html: Backups are the only real safety net for irreversible operations — and only if they are recent, tested (an untested backup is a hypothesis), and actually restorable. Verify all three before any risky change, not after.
m4.lessons.2.blocks.6.html: Decide whether and when the product can safely absorb this migration. What happens to existing rows? How long are locks held? What can be rolled back? Has the backup been restored successfully? Rehearse on representative disposable data and explain any downtime or irreversible loss to the people approving the change.
m4.lessons.2.title: Migrations & the point of no return
m4.tagline: Keep data useful, consistent, and recoverable as the product grows.

m5.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: Every import is an edge. Starting from entry points, the runtime or bundler resolves each edge — relative paths, package names, aliases — building a dependency graph. Bundlers then fold the graph into files and drop the parts that are provably unused (tree shaking).
m5.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Cycles break that clean picture: A imports B, B imports A. Depending on where initialization starts, one module can see the other half-initialized — which is how you get undefined at import time, errors that vanish when imports are reordered, and tests that only pass together.
m5.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: Architecture is enforceable here: lint rules can ban imports by path (no data importing UI, no module reaching past the service layer), and dependency-graph tools can visualize cycles or fail CI on them. A convention in a document is advice; an import rule in CI is a wall.
m5.deeper.0.title: How your build system walks the import graph
m5.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: The model never reads your repository. On every turn, the harness assembles a context: system instructions, your rules file, the open files, retrieved snippets, and tool output — all packed into a fixed token budget. Anything outside it does not exist for that call.
m5.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: This is why conventions drift and generic-correct code appears: with no visibility into the rest of the codebase, the model falls back to its training average. It is also why long sessions degrade — as the context fills, early instructions get less attention, and material in the middle is recalled worse than the beginning and end.
m5.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: put the rules where the context will actually include them (a rules file, an exemplar path), keep sessions short and focused, and never assume the agent remembers a decision it made an hour ago. Context is a budget, not memory.
