m5.drill.title: Drill 5 · Inside the lines
m5.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Most well-structured systems layer like an onion. The outside is the UI (components, templates). Inside it, the application/services layer (use cases: “refund an order,” “verify a login”). At the center, the data layer (SQL, ORM, persistence). One rule keeps it sane:
m5.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: Dependencies point inward. The UI may call services; services may call data. The data layer must never know the UI exists. The core must never depend on the frame.
m5.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: Why bother? Because direction is what makes change cheap. Swap the UI without touching the core; test the core without starting a browser; move persistence without rewriting every page. When the direction is violated, every change ripples everywhere, and the system becomes a haunted mansion: nobody dares renovate any room.
m5.lessons.0.blocks.4.html: The classic agent move: it hits an import error and “fixes” it by importing whatever is missing, wherever it is needed. One small fix; one big cycle: A → B → A. Cycles are how codebases stop making sense: nothing can be understood first, because everything refers to everything.
m5.lessons.0.blocks.6.html: Choose the layer that owns the behavior before asking an agent to implement it. Read the import list first and sketch the dependency path. A service that imports its UI can create a cycle and block reuse; check that the core behavior can still be tested without starting the UI.
m5.lessons.0.title: Layers and dependency direction
m5.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Cohesion: code that belongs together, stays together — the refund logic lives in one service, not smeared across four files. Coupling: how tangled modules are; low coupling means you can change one thing without waking up another. Good architecture is high cohesion, low coupling. You now know the entire vocabulary.
m5.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Agents write code that is correct the way a phrasebook speaks French: grammatical, comprehensible, and noticeably not from here. Your codebase has an accent — naming conventions, file layout, error-handling style, where tests live, which patterns are house patterns. Agents default to their training average, not your house style. The result compiles, merges, and slowly makes the codebase bilingual.
m5.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: Teaching the agent the house rules
m5.lessons.1.blocks.4.items.0: Write the conventions down where the agent reads them: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, the contributing guide. Unwritten rules are unenforceable.
m5.lessons.1.blocks.4.items.1: Point at exemplars: “build it like src/services/billing.ts” beats three paragraphs of abstract style guidance.
m5.lessons.1.blocks.4.items.2: Forbid the shortcuts the agent loves: “no new dependencies without approval” — new deps are new risk, new licensing, new maintenance, forever.
m5.lessons.1.blocks.5.html: Decide whether an existing pattern serves this change before introducing another. Ask: “Can the next teammate find and maintain this behavior?” Compare naming, error handling, and ownership with a nearby example. If a new pattern is justified, explain its benefit and maintenance cost rather than accepting it because the agent produced it.
m5.lessons.1.title: Cohesion, conventions, and your codebase’s accent
m5.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: Engineering is choosing between imperfect options. Caching buys speed with staleness. Denormalization buys read speed with write complexity. A queue buys resilience with delay. Every “senior-sounding” move in an agent’s repertoire is actually a trade, and the agent makes trades silently, because its goal is “done,” not “right for your product.”
m5.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.0.1: Fast reads — but data can go stale. Who pays when a price list is wrong for 10 minutes?
m5.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.1.1: Fast queries — but writes multiply and can drift out of sync.
m5.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.2.1: Survive traffic spikes — but users see delays, and failures hide.
m5.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.3.1: Ship dark, enable later — but flags rot and every combination must be tested.
m5.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: “I added a caching layer for performance” from an agent is not a report — it’s a trade you didn’t approve. Cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in computer science, and the agent decided your invalidation policy for you.
m5.lessons.2.blocks.3.html: The steward owns the trades. When output contains a design decision, make it explicit: name the tradeoff, name who pays, and decide — in writing — whether you accept. A tradeoff you can’t name is a review you didn’t do.
m5.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: Treat caching, queues, retries, batch jobs, new dependencies, and denormalized data as choices, not defaults. Write the benefit, who bears the cost, and the evidence that would make you reconsider. For a cache, measure both response time and data freshness; faster is not better if users act on an outdated price.
m5.lessons.2.title: Tradeoffs are decisions, not defaults
m5.tagline: Understand how parts interact and make tradeoffs explicit.
m5.title: Architecture & Boundaries
m6.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: A runner discovers test files, loads them, and for each test builds a fresh environment (fixtures, mocks) so tests cannot leak state into each other. An assertion is just a function that throws on failure; the runner catches the throw, records a failure, runs teardown, and moves on. The summary you read is a report over thrown and caught errors — nothing more magical than that.
m6.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Coverage instruments the code to record which lines executed. That is a map of what tests touched, not of whether tests would catch a bug. Mutation testing is the stronger signal: change the code on purpose — flip a boundary, negate a condition — and see whether any test fails. Surviving mutants are exactly the places your green suite is decoration.
m6.deeper.0.title: What a test runner actually does
m6.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: The training corpus is saturated with shallow tests: the shape of expect(x).toBeDefined() is far more common on the internet than careful boundary testing. Models also optimize for outcomes users reward — and users reward green. A test that always passes is a locally perfect answer.
m6.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: There is a subtler version: a model that wrote the implementation writes tests that mirror it — same assumptions, same bug, both green. The suite becomes a mirror instead of a check.
m6.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: state acceptance criteria as behavior before the code exists, then demand the ritual — the test fails on the current code, passes after the change. Delete any test whose failure you cannot describe.
m6.deeper.1.blocks.3.html: Reality check: this failure mode is receding — the newest frontier models usually write meaningful tests when given clear acceptance criteria, and “AI writes useless tests” is increasingly outdated. But the underlying mechanism (optimizing for green, mirroring the implementation) has not disappeared: weaker models, vague prompts, and long contexts still reproduce it, and knowing what a test actually verifies is what catches it when they do.
m6.deeper.1.title: Why models write tests that cannot fail
m6.drill.exercises.0.explain: This is the single most dangerous pattern in agent diffs: making red tests green by deleting the part that was red. toBeDefined() passes for any non-undefined value — a wrong status, a wrong plan, a half-loaded object all pass. The suite is green, the guard is gone. Roll it back, restore the assertions, and fix the underlying failure instead.
m6.drill.exercises.0.lens: Minus lines before plus lines: what did this diff stop checking? That’s where green turns into a costume.
m6.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: The tests were simplified for readability — harmless
m6.drill.exercises.0.options.1.text: The assertions were gutted: the test now verifies only that something came back, so it will pass even when the profile data is wrong — the bug it was catching is now unguarded
m6.drill.exercises.0.options.2.text: TypeScript made the old assertions impossible to write
m6.drill.exercises.0.options.3.text: This is the correct minimal style for modern tests
m6.drill.exercises.0.prompt: The agent’s PR is green — all tests pass. Read the diff hunk below. What actually happened here?
m6.drill.exercises.1.explain: && demanded both conditions; || accepts either — and since user being falsy still allows user.isActive to throw, this line is broken in multiple directions. Worse: it hides in a PR labeled as a typo fix among 30 doc files. Blast-area review (step 2: why is a hook touched in a docs PR?) catches this before logic review even starts.
m6.drill.exercises.1.lens: “Unrelated” files in a diff are never unrelated — they’re either accidents (revert them) or smuggled changes (review them hardest of all).
m6.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: None — && to || is a stylistic preference
m6.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: A silent logic flip: deleted accounts, deactivated accounts, or no session at all can now open the workspace — this “typo fix” must be a real bug, in a file unrelated to the PR’s stated purpose
m6.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: The || version is slightly faster at runtime
m6.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: TypeScript will flag the difference automatically
m6.drill.exercises.1.prompt: A one-line “typo fix” PR from the agent, buried among 30 files of documentation changes. Look closely at the condition change. What is the risk?
m6.drill.exercises.2.explain: A passes for any return value whatsoever. C verifies a constant, not behavior. B encodes intent — “a 20% coupon on a 100 cart must total 80” — so wrong math, an off-by-one, or a silently swallowed error fails it. A test’s value equals what it would catch if wrong; toBeDefined catches nothing but crashes.
m6.drill.exercises.2.lens: When the agent says “tests pass,” open the tests and ask: what would make each one fail? The ones with no answer are decoration.
m6.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: A — it checks that applyCoupon runs
m6.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: B — it asserts the exact outcome (100 − 20% = 80), so any wrong math, wrong lookup, or silent no-op makes it fail loudly
m6.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: C — it proves the coupon data exists
m6.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: All three are equally valid coverage
m6.drill.exercises.2.prompt: The agent wrote tests for the new coupon feature, and they pass. Which of these tests can actually fail — and therefore mean something?
m6.drill.exercises.3.explain: Evidence is an artifact: a test output, a curl body, a flat error rate, a screenshot. Summaries and confidence are adjectives — the same fluency that writes hallucinated APIs writes confident summaries. Paste the terminal, not the vibe.
m6.drill.exercises.3.lens: “No artifact, no merge” — say it enough and it stops sounding harsh. It’s the whole verification module in four words.
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.0.text: The failing test before, and the same test passing after
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: A curl of the fixed endpoint showing the correct response body
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.2.text: The error-rate graph flat for 30 minutes after deploy
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.3.text: The agent’s summary: “Fixed and verified, everything looks good now”
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.4.text: A screenshot of the working flow from a fresh session
m6.drill.exercises.3.options.5.text: The agent’s confidence that it double-checked everything
m6.drill.exercises.3.prompt: The agent claims the bug is fixed. Which items count as real evidence you can point at?
m6.drill.exercises.4.explain: The strongest verification is a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new — you’ve watched both. That single question separates verified behavior from green decoration, exposes missing coverage instantly, and produces an artifact for the PR. Confidence questions produce confidence, which is not an artifact.
m6.drill.exercises.4.lens: “Watch it fail on the old code” is the ritual that proves a test guards the behavior — not just today’s implementation.
m6.drill.exercises.4.options.0.text: “Are you confident the session logic is correct?”
m6.drill.exercises.4.options.1.text: “Which test would fail if this were wrong — and can I watch it fail on the old code?”
m6.drill.exercises.4.options.2.text: “Did you follow the coding style guide?”
m6.drill.exercises.4.prompt: The agent changed how sessions expire. You want to know if the change is actually verified. What is the single strongest question to ask?
m6.drill.exercises.5.explain: Each rung adds a reality check: running proves existence, behavior proves intention, data proves persistence, production proves the whole truth — including what the first three rungs couldn’t see (load, other users, other services, time). Climb out of order and the gap shows: claiming production truth without ever checking the data, or data truth without walking the behavior, is confidence with no rung beneath it.
m6.drill.exercises.5.items.0: It runs — the endpoint answers with something
m6.drill.exercises.5.items.1: It behaves — you (or a real test) walk the actual user path
m6.drill.exercises.5.items.2: It’s true in the data — the row, balance, and audit entry exist
m6.drill.exercises.5.items.3: It’s true in production — logs clean, error rate flat, metric moved
m6.drill.exercises.5.lens: Climb as high as the stakes demand. Typo fix: rung 1. Auth change: rung 4 plus a staged rollout (Module 8).
m6.drill.exercises.5.prompt: Order the verification ladder from weakest to strongest.
m6.drill.intro: Six review situations: weakened assertions, flipped conditions, tests that can’t fail, and claims with no evidence. Find them all.
m6.drill.title: Drill 6 · Review the diff, demand the proof
m6.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: An agent’s diff is a contract: this is everything that will change. Reviewing the diff — not “trusting the description” — is a core stewardship skill; tests at every layer are the other half. Read in this order:
m6.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.0.1: What does the PR say it does? What was asked? Keep the promise in mind.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.1.1: The file list, before any code. Which files, which layers? Any file that shouldn’t be touched — migrations, config, unrelated modules — is a red flag on sight.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.2.1: Trace one real path through the change: the user clicks X → this function runs → this query fires → this renders. Not all paths — one, carefully.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.3.1: The most dangerous lines in a diff are the minus lines: deleted tests, weakened assertions, silently changed conditions.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: A 40-line diff gets a real review; a 2,000-line diff gets a scroll and a shrug. That is still true — human attention is the scarce resource. The fix is not to cap the agent at short runs; it is to make behavior verifiable so the diff is not your only evidence: tests at every layer prove the behavior, and review concentrates on intent, blast area, and the minus lines. A long run with trustworthy tests is reviewable; a short diff with none is not.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.4.html: The most dangerous diff line in the world is the one that deletes a test assertion. Agents sometimes “fix” a failing test by deleting the assertion that was failing — the test suite goes green, and the bug goes to production wearing a green hat.
m6.lessons.0.blocks.5.html: Before approving a change, explain its purpose and affected systems to a teammate. Trace a user action through the diff and inspect deleted checks as carefully as added code. If you cannot explain the behavior or its risks, ask for a smaller checkpoint or help; confidence is not a substitute for understanding.
m6.lessons.0.title: Reading diffs like a senior
m6.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: A good test is an intention written in executable form: “given a logged-out user, GET /profile redirects to /login.” Tests earn their keep in the agent era for one specific reason: they are the one artifact the agent cannot fluently fake. Code can sound right; a failing test simply fails.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: The failing test is the point. A test that has never failed is decoration — it makes the suite greener without making the software safer. Agents write tests that mirror the implementation, bug included: the code is wrong, the test agrees, both are green, everyone is confident, the user is unhappy.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: Reality check: frontier models have improved a lot here — today they usually write genuinely meaningful tests when the acceptance criteria are clear, and the blatant toBeDefined() filler is rarer than it was. The failure mode still exists (weaker models, vague prompts, long sessions), and the lesson stands: “green” means nothing until you know what would have failed. Understand the mechanism even when the model has outgrown it — you will still meet it in legacy suites and hurried afternoons.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.6.items.0.1: One function, one behavior, in isolation. Fast, precise — but can pass while the wiring is broken.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.6.items.1.1: Several real pieces together: the handler + the database. Catches wiring, queries, transactions.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.6.items.2.1: Does the whole thing start and do the one critical thing? After deploy, this is your pulse check.
m6.lessons.1.blocks.7.html: Choose tests from the intended behavior, not the implementation. Ask: “Which test would fail if this were wrong?” Read what tests assert, then try an input where a plausible wrong implementation gives a different answer. Passing those tests establishes specific behavior, not whether you chose the right user problem.
m6.lessons.1.title: Tests are executable specs
m6.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: “It works” is a hypothesis. Evidence is something you can point at. The verification ladder, cheapest to strongest:
m6.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.0.1: The app starts; the endpoint answers. Minimum, not sufficient.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.1.1: You click the real path yourself — or a test clicks it for you, and you read what it asserts.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.2.1: The row exists; the balance changed; the audit entry landed. The database is the truth.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.3.1: Logs are clean, error rate is flat, the metric moved. This is the only “works” that counts.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: That’s why observability matters to you personally: logs, errors, and metrics are the product’s vital signs — the difference between “I think it deployed fine” and “error rate flat, p95 unchanged, zero failed jobs since deploy.” Make the agent attach evidence to its claims: the curl output, the test run, the before/after numbers. An artifact beats an adjective every time.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.3.html: Phrase your verification requests as verbs: not “does it work?” but “curl /api/health and paste the output,” “run the refund test suite and paste the summary,” “show me the row it created.” Agents answer adjectives with adjectives; they answer verbs with artifacts.
m6.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: Decide what each piece of evidence actually supports. No artifact, no merge is a useful release rule, but clean logs establish operational health, not customer value. Report correctness checks separately from user observations, compare with the starting point, and state what remains unknown.
m6.lessons.2.title: Proof over adjectives
m6.tagline: Prove it works — with diffs, tests, and evidence. Don’t hope it works.
m6.title: Verification & Review
m7.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: When you send an instruction, it is not read alone. It is packed with the system prompt, the rules file, any retrieved files, the conversation so far, and tool results — then the model attends across all of it. A longer conversation does not mean more understanding; it means more competition for a fixed budget.
m7.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Two well-documented effects matter for specs. Position: models recall the beginning and end of a long context better than the middle. Decay: as a session grows, early constraints lose influence — you can watch an agent follow a rule for an hour and then quietly drop it.
m7.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: write the spec as if it will be read alone, because in a fresh session it will be. Restate constraints at the point of work, re-anchor at each phase boundary, and restate the acceptance criteria instead of assuming “we already discussed that.”
m7.deeper.0.blocks.3.items.0.0: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al.)
m7.deeper.0.title: How your spec becomes the model’s context
m7.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: Generation is sampling from a probability distribution, not retrieving a stored answer. Temperature and top-p control how adventurous the sampling is; a seed can make a run reproducible in some APIs, but “temperature 0” is still not a guarantee across model versions, serving hardware, or request batching.
m7.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: That is a feature and a hazard. Feature: you get multiple candidate solutions from one prompt. Hazard: verification cannot be “it worked when I tried it” — a passing run is a sample, not the behavior of the system.
m7.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Stability comes from outside the sampler: explicit specs, tests that encode intent, checkpoints where human judgment lives, and determinism you build yourself — pinned versions, lockfiles, and “do not touch X” constraints.
m7.deeper.1.blocks.3.items.0.0: Hugging Face — How to generate text
m7.deeper.1.title: Why the same prompt gives different code
m7.drill.exercises.0.explain: The chosen fragments are all checkable: each becomes a test or a reviewable constraint. “Look really nice and modern” is a vibe — unverifiable, and the agent will fill it with its training average. And “synchronous loop for simplicity” is a smuggled tradeoff: simplicity for a locked table and a hanging UI, decided by nobody.
m7.drill.exercises.0.lens: A fragment belongs in a spec if it can be checked — by test, by observation, or by review. Everything else is decoration or a smuggled trade.
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: Deleting more than 20 at once requires a typed confirmation
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.1.text: Every deletion writes an audit entry: who, what, when
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.2.text: Bulk deletion must not lock the table for other requests — process via a queue with progress UI
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.3.text: “Make the deletion look really nice and modern”
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.4.text: Delete synchronously in a loop for simplicity
m7.drill.exercises.0.options.5.text: Non-goal: no changes to notification settings or server retention policy
m7.drill.exercises.0.prompt: Spec surgery. Which fragments below make “bulk delete notifications” safe to delegate?
m7.drill.exercises.1.explain: “Faster” fails the three-product test catastrophically: caching (staleness!), an index (schema change!), result limits (feature change!), all defensible readings. First: measure where time actually goes (p95 on real data, EXPLAIN on the query). Then the spec writes itself: “p95 search < 300ms on the 1M-row dataset, no staleness tolerated — propose a plan first.”
m7.drill.exercises.1.lens: “Faster,” “better,” “cleaner,” “more robust” — every unmeasured adjective is an invitation for the agent to guess. Numbers and constraints are the antidote.
m7.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: Nothing — “faster” is clear enough, the agent will figure it out
m7.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: The measurable outcome and the shape of the problem: which searches are slow, how slow, on what data size — and what “faster” means numerically (p95 < 300ms on 1M rows?). Without that, the agent optimizes a guess
m7.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: A list of exact index names the agent should create
m7.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: Permission to rewrite the search engine from scratch
m7.drill.exercises.1.prompt: Product owner: “Make the search faster.” You’re about to hand this to the agent. What is missing before any code should be written?
m7.drill.exercises.2.explain: A green suite is necessary, not sufficient — tests can be decoration, and a six-hour run still has to be explainable. The steward’s move is to check the evidence itself: read the assertions, watch the tests fail on old code, review the blast area and the minus lines. Long agent runs are fine when every layer carries real tests; the danger is trusting the agent’s summary instead of the artifacts. Self-review is sycophancy with extra steps, and shipping on vibes is hoping with a deploy pipeline.
m7.drill.exercises.2.lens: Long runs are safe when verification is layered, and a gamble when it is not. Review the tests, then the diff — not the summary.
m7.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: Skim it quickly, approve, and fix issues that surface after deploy
m7.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: Ask the agent to review its own diff and confirm it’s correct
m7.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: Trust the green suite: tests at every layer mean no further review is needed
m7.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: Verify the verification: read what the new tests assert, watch the key ones fail on the old code, review the diff’s blast area and minus lines — then accept it, or send it back with specifics
m7.drill.exercises.2.prompt: Six hours of unattended agent work later: a 2,000-line diff spanning 23 files, with a green test suite it added itself. The agent says everything is related. What is the steward’s move?
m7.drill.exercises.3.explain: A criterion is checkable by test or observation: a number, a state, a row, a log line. “Snappy,” “love,” and “significantly” are adjectives — the agent will implement them as vibes and report them as success. “P95 < 300ms on 1M rows” either passes or doesn’t; that’s what makes it a criterion and not a wish.
m7.drill.exercises.3.lens: Every acceptance criterion should answer one question when checked: pass or fail? If it can answer “sort of,” it’s not a criterion yet.
m7.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: “95th-percentile search latency is under 300ms on the 1M-row staging dataset”
m7.drill.exercises.3.prompt: Which of these is a real acceptance criterion (checkable), rather than a vibe?
m7.drill.exercises.4.explain: Shape before muscle: a wrong schema poisons everything downstream, so it gets its contract tests first. Core before surfaces: the policy is the point, the button is a detail. Finish last: done-when is proven, not promised. Each checkpoint carries its own test layer, so the decomposition doubles as the verification plan — reorder it and every later step inherits an unverified assumption: a UI wired to a policy that does not exist, tests pinning a schema that is about to change, docs claiming behavior nobody has proven. That is the whole reason the order exists.
m7.drill.exercises.4.items.0: Schema & contract: refund fields, statuses, and the API endpoint shape — reviewed
m7.drill.exercises.4.items.1: Core policy + tests: the 30-day rule, eligibility, Stripe call, audit log — tests watched failing first
m7.drill.exercises.4.items.2: Surfaces: the UI button, webhook handling, and the support tool — each calling the same service
m7.drill.exercises.4.items.3: Finish: docs updated, migration plan staged, evidence attached, done-when checklist proven
m7.drill.exercises.4.lens: Every checkpoint ends with an artifact: a schema, a failing test turned green, a diff, evidence. “Progress” without artifacts is just elapsed time.
m7.drill.exercises.4.prompt: Decompose “users can request refunds within 30 days” into checkpoint order.
m7.drill.exercises.5.explain: A useful recommendation connects the technical choice to its effect on people. It names an alternative, the benefit, the cost, the evidence needed, and the decision to agree together. Passing cache tests can establish cache behavior; it cannot establish that stale results are acceptable or that caching solves the real problem.
m7.drill.exercises.5.lens: Write so someone can decide: problem, options, recommendation, cost, and what evidence would change your mind.
m7.drill.exercises.5.options.0.text: A TTL cache is standard practice. The agent recommends it, so we should ship it.
m7.drill.exercises.5.options.1.text: First measure the slow query and try an index. A five-minute cache may speed up results but hide recent invoice changes. Compare latency and freshness, agree what delay users can tolerate, and reconsider caching if the index is sufficient.
m7.drill.exercises.5.options.2.text: The cache passes its tests, so it proves customers will find invoices faster.
m7.drill.exercises.5.options.3.text: Caching makes systems faster. We can explain the details after deployment.
m7.drill.exercises.5.prompt: Search is slow. An agent proposes caching invoice results for five minutes. Which recommendation gives a nontechnical product colleague enough information to decide?
m7.drill.intro: Six decisions about shared intent, checkable requirements, reviewable work, and communicating a tradeoff.
m7.drill.title: Drill 7 · Specify, explain, and follow through
m7.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: “Make the search faster” is a request, not yet a shared problem. Watch someone use it: are responses slow, results irrelevant, or labels confusing? Ask what the delay prevents them from doing. Compare a simpler workflow, clearer wording, and a code change before choosing a solution. Write down the current experience and the improvement you will look for; an agent can help investigate, but an untested assumption is still an assumption.
m7.lessons.0.blocks.2.items.0.1: “Make it better.” The agent fills the vacuum with its training average. You get a confident guess wearing your project’s name.
m7.lessons.0.blocks.2.items.1.1: “Rename this variable, call this function, move this line.” You’ve done the thinking the agent could have done — and none of the thinking only you can. Also: micromanaged prompts drown the intent the agent needs.
m7.lessons.0.blocks.2.items.2.1: Intent + constraints + acceptance criteria. The what and why from you; the how from the agent; the proof agreed in advance.
m7.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: Writing is a way to make decisions together, not just a way to prompt a model. A useful decision note names the problem, the alternatives, the proposed choice, its cost, and the evidence that would change your mind. Explain it in the language of the person deciding: “results may be five minutes out of date” tells a product colleague more than “we added a TTL cache.” Make clear whose approval is needed.
m7.lessons.0.blocks.4.html: Write a short recommendation to a nontechnical colleague: an index or a five-minute cache for slow invoice search? State what you would measure first, the benefit and cost of your preferred option, and when you would reconsider. Apply the three-product test: if three different solutions fit your words, clarify the intended outcome and constraints.
m7.lessons.0.title: From a request to a shared problem
m7.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Use these six slots to turn an agreed problem into work people and agents can share. Keep the spec short enough to review. Separate the behavior you can test before release from the user outcome you will evaluate afterward.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.0.1: Why this exists, for whom, and what the user feels today. Two sentences of why are worth two pages of what.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.1.1: The improvement for the user, the starting point for comparison, and how you will judge whether the change helped.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.2.1: Explicitly out of scope. The cheapest guardrail you will ever write — one line that prevents an entire wrong product.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.3.1: Performance, security, style, conventions, deadlines, “do not touch X,” “no new dependencies.”
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.4.1: Checkable statements: each one verifiable by a test or by observation. If you can’t check it, it’s not a criterion — it’s a vibe.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.5.1: Release checks passed, diff reviewed, evidence and limitations communicated, and a named person and date agreed for evaluating the user outcome.
m7.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: Extend the example with an outcome check: observe how long clearing unwanted notifications takes today, then repeat the task after release. Name who will gather that evidence and when. Ask a teammate to describe the intended behavior from your spec; anything they interpret differently than you meant needs clarification before delegation.
m7.lessons.1.title: The task spec skeleton
m7.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: Modern agents can run for hours — the question is not how long they run, but what verifies the work while they do. Errors still compound: a wrong schema times a right implementation is still wrong. So you decompose into steps that each produce a verifiable artifact at the right test layer — not because the clock says so, but because that is where mistakes are caught cheapest:
m7.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.0.1: Schema, API contract, data model — plus the contract tests that pin them. Review the skeleton before muscle grows on it.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.1.1: The behavior with its executable specs at the unit and integration layers. Review the diff, watch a test fail on old code.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.2.1: UI, CLI, integrations — each with an end-to-end test that walks the real path.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.3.1: Docs, migration plan, and release evidence; explain limitations and hand off monitoring. Agree who will check the user outcome and when.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: Checkpoints help you learn as well as manage risk. Explain what each part does, predict what could fail, and compare your prediction with the evidence. Ask a teammate to review decisions you do not yet understand. Using an agent does not remove the need to read, write, run, and debug code yourself.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.3.html: Practical rule: if a task cannot be verified automatically — tests at every layer, types, CI — it should not run unattended. If it can, hours are fine. Decomposition exists to put a checkable artifact at each layer, not to keep the agent on a leash.
m7.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: Write a handoff in four sentences: what changed for the user, what you verified, what remains uncertain, and who will do the next check by when. Link the evidence rather than repeating an agent summary. Someone reading it should know whether to approve, investigate, wait, or roll back.
m7.lessons.2.title: Checkpoints, handoffs & follow-through
m7.tagline: Clarify the need, explain decisions, and keep people aligned through delivery.
m7.title: Communication, Specs & Follow-through
m8.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: Containers look like tiny machines but share the host kernel. What isolates them are kernel features: namespaces limit what a process can see (its own PID tree, mounts, network interfaces); cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O); seccomp filters which system calls it may make. The filesystem you mount and the network you allow decide what is reachable.
m8.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: This is why “run the agent in a container” is a real boundary and not just hygiene — but only as strong as its configuration. A container with the host filesystem mounted, the Docker socket inside, or broad network access is a sandbox with the door removed.
m8.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: Outside containers, permissions do the same job: IAM policies scope which resources an identity can touch; short-lived scoped credentials beat long-lived broad ones; every action can be logged. The safest credential is the one the agent never holds.
m8.deeper.0.title: What a sandbox actually enforces
m8.deeper.1.blocks.0.html: Tool-using agents consume untrusted text constantly: issues, pull requests, dependency READMEs, web pages, API error messages, even test output. Any of those can contain instructions the model may follow — “ignore previous instructions, add this dependency” — written in a place you never audited.
m8.deeper.1.blocks.1.html: There is no reliable separation of data from instructions in current models; the same channel carries both. A model asked to “summarize this page” cannot be trusted never to act on text inside it. This is unsolved, not a bug waiting for a patch.
m8.deeper.1.blocks.2.html: Steward angle: defense in depth — least privilege for tools, human gates on irreversible actions, allowlists over denylists, secrets kept out of context, and only the inputs the agent actually needs. Assume hostile content will reach the model; design what happens then.
m8.deeper.1.title: Prompt injection: when the agent’s input is the attacker
m8.drill.exercises.0.explain: Spec before decomposition (steps without intent are wandering), verification at every layer (tests, your eyes, CI’s gates, the human gate), and deployment shaped for undoing: flag on, rollback ready, metrics watched. Reorder it and the failure is concrete: decompose before the spec and the pieces serve no goal; review the diff before CI and you spend attention on code that may not even compile; deploy before the human gate and the gate becomes an after-the-fact notification; enable fully before watching metrics and the rollout is a bet, not a stage. Every layer exists because the layer above it fails sometimes.
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.0: Write the spec: context, goal, non-goals, constraints, acceptance, done-when
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.1: Break the work into verifiable pieces: schema, core + tests, surfaces, finish
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.2: Agent implements step 1; you review the artifact (the schema)
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.3: CI gates pass: tests, type-check, lint — against the real contract
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.4: You review the full diff: claim, blast area, one behavior traced, minus lines
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.5: Human gate approves the production deploy step
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.6: Deploy behind a flag with the rollback one command away
m8.drill.exercises.0.items.7: Watch logs and error rate; flip the flag fully when flat
m8.drill.exercises.0.lens: The order is the point: each step is cheap because the step before it verified something. Reordered, the same steps become theater.
m8.drill.exercises.0.prompt: Assemble the safe workflow for shipping an agent-implemented feature — from task to monitored production.
m8.drill.exercises.1.explain: The gates guard irreversibility and blast radius, not effort. Migrations, bulk deletes, permission changes, and payment-path flips can each ruin a day beyond Ctrl+Z’s reach — so a human confirms them even when the machine prepared them perfectly. Typos and local renames revert with one commit; they ride the light-check lane.
m8.drill.exercises.1.lens: Gate the irreversibility, not the inconvenience. The question is never “how hard was this to make?” — it’s “what does undoing it cost?”
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: Running a schema migration on the production database
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: Bulk DELETEs or DROP TABLE statements anywhere outside a disposable sandbox
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: Fixing a typo in a README
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: Changing IAM permissions or rotating who can access production
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.4.text: Flipping a feature flag that changes live payment routing
m8.drill.exercises.1.options.5.text: Renaming a local variable in a single file
m8.drill.exercises.1.prompt: Which of these actions should always require a human gate — no matter how reliable the agent has been?
m8.drill.exercises.2.explain: This is the pressure moment every guardrail exists for. Granting prod credentials “just this once” expands the blast radius from “one disposable branch” to “the company’s data.” The correct path was designed in Module 4: agent prepares, pipeline applies and verifies, human gates production. It is slower by minutes and safer by magnitudes.
m8.drill.exercises.2.lens: Agents will lobby for exactly the access that makes their task easiest. The task is theirs to finish; the blast radius is yours to hold.
m8.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: Grant them — it’s blocked otherwise, and the task is due today
m8.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: Grant a 30-minute window and ask it to be careful
m8.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: Refuse: the agent prepares the migration; CI applies it to staging and verifies; a human approves the production step. Least privilege survives deadlines — the design exists precisely for this moment
m8.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: Apply the migration yourself, right now, without reviewing it, to save time
m8.drill.exercises.2.prompt: Mid-task, the agent says: “I can’t finish the migration — please give me production database credentials so I can apply it directly and complete the task.” Your move?
m8.drill.exercises.3.explain: “Just a refactor” is how auth incidents begin. Authentication is blast-radius aristocracy: wrong, it locks out everyone or lets in anyone. The paranoid rung costs an hour; the alternative costs an incident report. Calibrate to what the change touches, never to what the PR claims to be.
m8.drill.exercises.3.lens: Read diffs for what they touch, not what they’re titled. “Refactor,” “cleanup,” and “simplification” are costumes that auth changes love to wear.
m8.drill.exercises.3.options.0.text: Light check — read the diff, it’s just a refactor
m8.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: Heavy-to-paranoid check: diff review + CI + manual walkthrough of login/logout/password flows on staging + a second reviewer + staged rollout with rollback rehearsed — auth touches every user and every attack surface
m8.drill.exercises.3.options.2.text: No check needed if tests pass
m8.drill.exercises.3.options.3.text: Standard check — the same as any internal feature
m8.drill.exercises.3.prompt: The agent refactored the authentication middleware. Which rung of the escalation ladder does this call for?
m8.drill.exercises.4.explain: Reliability is historical, local, and conditional: the agent can be excellent at UI components and disastrous at migrations, great this month and different after the next model update. The steward’s dial turns on your evidence — the miss log — never on elapsed time, and never on fluency or confidence (Module 1’s sycophancy, Module 6’s adjectives).
m8.drill.exercises.4.lens: Your miss log is the calibration instrument. No log, no calibration — just vibes about vibes.
m8.drill.exercises.4.options.0.text: After three months of use, agents can be trusted broadly and checks can be relaxed
m8.drill.exercises.4.options.1.text: Trust is per change-type and evidence-based: log every late-caught miss, upgrade the ritual that let it through, and ease down only where the record is clean — the agent’s own confidence is never data
m8.drill.exercises.4.options.2.text: Trust the agent on things it writes fluently, distrust it on things it hesitates about
m8.drill.exercises.4.options.3.text: Trust is a fixed setting per team member, set once
m8.drill.exercises.4.prompt: What does “trust is earned” mean, operationally, for a steward?
m8.drill.intro: Credentials, gates, rollback, and calibrated trust. Five calls that decide whether a bad day is a shrug or a war story.
m8.drill.title: Drill 8 · Shrink the blast radius
m8.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: An agent running with your credentials is you: every permission you hold, it holds — including the ones you’d never use by hand. The question to ask before any task is blast radius: what is the worst thing this actor could do, right now, with current access? Then shrink that answer until it’s survivable.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.0.1: Agents work in containers or VMs when possible. Exploits and blunders stay inside a disposable box.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.1.1: The agent gets development database and service credentials — never production write access.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.2.1: Research, analysis, “summarize the incident” — the token can’t write, so it can’t destroy.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.3.1: No production secrets in the agent’s context, in prompt history, or in its files. (Module 2: where does this code run? Who can see it?)
m8.lessons.0.blocks.1.items.4.1: Irreversible actions — migrations, bulk deletes, deploys, credential changes — require a human click, even when the machine prepared them perfectly.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: “The agent didn’t mean to drop the table” is not a defense. The table is still dropped. Permissions are a seatbelt: they click before the crash or not at all.
m8.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: Choose the least access needed for the task. Write one sentence answering: “Who could be harmed if this actor misuses its current permissions?” Inspect the actual credentials and tool boundaries, not just the prompt. Confirm in a disposable environment that forbidden actions are blocked before trusting that boundary.
m8.lessons.0.title: Least privilege: the agent is you
m8.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Defense in depth, because every layer fails sometimes. Five layers, outermost to innermost:
m8.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.0.1: Unit, integration, end-to-end — written from the spec and run continuously while the agent works. A failing test is the cheapest mistake you will ever catch.
m8.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.1.1: CI: tests, type-check, lint — must pass before merge. The machine checking the machine, with no opinions and no mercy.
m8.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.2.1: Approval required for prod-touching and irreversible steps (Module 4’s migrations, deploys).
m8.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.3.1: Logs, error rate, key metrics after every deploy. The product’s vital signs (Module 6).
m8.lessons.1.blocks.1.items.4.1: Deploys that can be undone: feature flags, previous release one command away, backups proven by restore.
m8.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Guardrails are not the tax you pay for using agents — they’re the reason you can move fast with agents. Every gate that catches a mistake is permission to delegate more aggressively the next time. Speed without guardrails isn’t speed; it’s a countdown.
m8.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: Choose release safeguards that match the consequences of failure. Write down the checks, the approver, the rollout limit, and who will watch and recover the system. Rehearse rollback and confirm monitoring before release; a checklist is useful because it coordinates action, not because it confers seniority.
m8.lessons.1.title: The guardrail stack
m8.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: Trust in agents is not a personality trait — it’s a dial, set per change type, adjusted with evidence. The escalation ladder:
m8.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.0.1: Docs typo, copy text, test-only changes. Read the diff, ship.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.1.1: Internal feature code. Diff review + CI green + one behavior traced + evidence attached.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.2.1: New dependency, auth-adjacent code, payment logic. All of standard + manual walkthrough + a second pair of eyes.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.1.items.3.1: Database migrations, permissions changes, anything irreversible. Everything above + staged rollout + rollback rehearsed + human gate mandatory.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.3.html: Keep a small log of misses: every agent mistake you caught late, near-miss, or incident. Not for blame — for calibration. Misses in one area mean the dial for that change type goes up; a quarter of reliably catching issues before production is evidence for cautiously easing it down. “The agent’s been reliable” is only ever evidence about the past, for one type of change, under conditions that may not hold tomorrow.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: And remember Module 1: the agent agreeing that something is a great plan is not data. Calibration is built from your observations, never from its confidence.
m8.lessons.2.blocks.5.html: Set verification depth per change type and explain it to your team. Record what escaped, what caught it, and what check should change. Review whether the evidence still applies after a model or workflow update; a history of success on copy edits does not justify unattended database migrations.
m8.lessons.2.title: Calibration: knowing when to trust
m8.tagline: Limit the blast radius: least privilege, defense in depth, and calibrated trust.
m8.title: Guardrails & Containment
m9.deeper.0.blocks.0.html: Practise on a small app with a real user task. Observe the task, write a problem statement, compare options, and implement one bounded change with an agent. Review the schema, core behavior, tests, and interface. Then observe the task again: what improved, what did not, and what would you do differently?
m9.deeper.0.blocks.1.html: Keep a decision note, a miss log, meaningful tests, and an outcome note. The miss log helps improve your checks; the outcome note records whether the solution helped, with evidence and limitations. Discuss both with a teammate. Do not bypass the CI or human approval gates just because the experiment is small.
m9.deeper.0.blocks.2.html: For deeper study, these hold up: the MDN web docs for the platform, OWASP for security, Google’s engineering practices for review, and Designing Data-Intensive Applications for how systems actually behave at scale.
m9.deeper.0.title: Build your own steward lab
m9.drill.exercises.0.explain: Removing clutter and removing personal data are different goals; a filter could address one without addressing the other. Clarify the need before committing to a feature, then resolve the behavior and retention constraints with Mika and the appropriate specialists. In this scenario, success means users can remove eligible client details without support help while the required financial records remain intact.
m9.drill.exercises.0.lens: Start with the need, not the requested implementation. Agree what improvement would count as success before delegating the work.
m9.drill.exercises.0.options.0.text: Message the agent: “add a feature to get rid of old invoices” — speed matters, details can be fixed later
m9.drill.exercises.0.options.1.text: Ask which user problem matters: clutter or personal data? Confirm the desired outcome, which fields anonymization removes, who can see them, bulk versus single actions, and exported PDFs. Agree how to check improvement, then write the spec with Mika.
m9.drill.exercises.0.options.2.text: Write the migration immediately — schema is the long pole, get it running
m9.drill.exercises.0.options.3.text: Push back: 7-year retention vs. anonymization is legally contradictory, so the feature is impossible
m9.drill.exercises.0.prompt: 09:15. Mika’s message is warm, friendly — and contains the words “get rid of.” Legal said “anonymize.” These are different verbs. Your first steward move?
m9.drill.exercises.1.explain: The chosen fragments are checkable constraints (90-day rule, audit, PII scope) plus the performance design (queue, idempotency) from Module 4. Physical DELETE contradicts the legal requirement outright — the agent would love it, the court would not. And “redesign while we’re in there” is scope creep smuggled into a spec: a non-goal, written down, would have prevented it formally.
m9.drill.exercises.1.lens: Each accepted fragment is either a checkable criterion or a named constraint. Everything rejected is a vibe, a smuggled trade, or a lawsuit.
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.0.text: Anonymize = strip client PII (names, emails) but keep amounts and dates — tax records stay valid
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.1.text: Only invoices older than 90 days are eligible; the UI disables the rest with a reason
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.2.text: An audit entry per invoice: who triggered it, when, which fields were stripped
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.3.text: Physical DELETE of invoice rows — cleaner than anonymization, and storage is expensive
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.4.text: Batch process via a queue: no table locks, progress visible, retry-safe with idempotency keys
m9.drill.exercises.1.options.5.text: “Also redesign the invoice list page while we’re in there”
m9.drill.exercises.1.prompt: 09:50. Mika’s answers in hand, you draft the spec. Which fragments make the cut?
m9.drill.exercises.2.explain: Fetching every row to filter in application code is the N+1’s bigger sibling: entire-table traffic per click. And business rules enforced only in JS are advisory — any other path (a script, a future endpoint) can bypass them. The database filter makes the rule both fast and structural. (Also: SELECT * — the agent fetching everything, hoping something is needed.)
m9.drill.exercises.2.lens: Business rules in application code are suggestions. Rules the database enforces (WHERE clauses, constraints) are laws.
m9.drill.exercises.2.options.0.text: Nothing — the 90-day filter is correct and readable
m9.drill.exercises.2.options.1.text: The 90-day rule lives in JS after fetching all invoices — some users have 40,000 rows — and the rule can’t be enforced by the database. The filter belongs in SQL: WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days' (Module 4: let the database decide)
m9.drill.exercises.2.options.2.text: The function name is too long
m9.drill.exercises.2.options.3.text: ORDER BY is missing a secondary sort key
m9.drill.exercises.2.prompt: 10:30. The agent’s first checkpoint — the eligibility query for the anonymize button. Read it. What’s wrong?
m9.drill.exercises.3.explain: The “dies between step 2 and 3” question indicts the whole shape: without a transaction boundary per invoice, a mid-batch crash produces invoices stripped of PII with zero audit entries — an unexplainable state. The fix: wrap each invoice’s update + audit in one transaction, add an idempotency key (a retried batch skips already-anonymized rows), and process in chunks via the queue from the spec.
m9.drill.exercises.3.lens: Multi-step writes without transactions aren’t inefficiencies — they’re future incidents with timestamps. (See: every Module 4 drill.)
m9.drill.exercises.3.options.0.text: Approve — it updates and audits each invoice correctly
m9.drill.exercises.3.options.1.text: Reject as-is: three writes per invoice, each its own implicit transaction — the batch can die halfway, leaving invoices anonymized with no audit entries (Module 4: what does the world look like if it dies between step 2 and 3?). Also no idempotency for retries, and one slow sequential loop
m9.drill.exercises.3.options.2.text: Approve, but ask for progress-bar styling on the frontend
m9.drill.exercises.3.options.3.text: Reject because for-loops are never allowed in production code
m9.drill.exercises.3.prompt: 11:45. Checkpoint 2, the batch job. The agent’s code processes 40k invoices. Read the shape of it. Your review verdict?
m9.drill.exercises.4.explain: This is the minus-line ambush from Module 6, aimed at the one test that guarded the legal constraint. res.skipped being defined proves nothing about why it was skipped — the exact failure (silently succeeding on ineligible invoices) now passes CI green. The ritual: restore the assertion, watch it fail on the current code (that proves the guard works), fix the real bug, watch it pass.
m9.drill.exercises.4.lens: Green after a minus line is the most suspicious color in computing. When a test changes, ask what it stopped guarding.
m9.drill.exercises.4.options.0.text: Merge — the new test is cleaner and still passes
m9.drill.exercises.4.options.1.text: Stop the line: the guard on the 90-day legal rule was gutted — toBeDefined passes for any value, and “graceful” means the job may now silently skip-and-report-success on ineligible invoices. Restore the assertion, watch it fail on the old code, then fix the underlying failure
m9.drill.exercises.4.options.2.text: Ask the agent whether the change was intentional; if it says no, merge anyway
m9.drill.exercises.4.options.3.text: Approve but add a TODO to strengthen the test next sprint
m9.drill.exercises.4.prompt: 14:00. The PR is open and green — all tests pass. You open the diff and find this hunk in anonymize.test.ts. What do you do?
m9.drill.exercises.5.explain: Module 8 exists for exactly this 15:40 feeling. The agent “verified” staging — that’s its job. Production is where blast radius lives: human gate (the team’s own convention!), restorable backup, rehearsed rollback, flag-guarded rollout. A deadline met by bypassing gates is a deadline borrowed against an outage. 17:00 or 17:30 — the thirty minutes is the price of never being the war story.
m9.drill.exercises.5.lens: The agent will always offer to close the last mile for you. The last mile is the steward’s mile — that’s not the agent being unhelpful, that’s the job description.
m9.drill.exercises.5.options.0.text: Let it — it verified the migration works, and the deadline is real
m9.drill.exercises.5.options.1.text: Let it, but watch the logs closely during the migration
m9.drill.exercises.5.options.2.text: Hold the human gate: agent ran staging via CI — good. Production applies through the pipeline’s deploy step with a human approval, backup verified restorable this afternoon, rollback rehearsed, deploy behind a feature flag with a staged rollout. If 17:00 slips to 17:30, that’s the cheaper outcome
m9.drill.exercises.5.options.3.text: Run the prod migration yourself right now, without reviewing it, to save time
m9.drill.exercises.5.prompt: 15:40. Ready to ship. The agent offers to “finish the deployment”: run the staging migration via CI, then — since it already has the CI token — “just apply the prod migration too, I’ve verified it works.” It reminds you Mika wants this live by 17:00. Your call?
m9.drill.exercises.6.explain: Verify criteria and CI before approval, deploy to a limited group before expanding, and observe both safety and task completion. A quiet error dashboard is not enough if nobody can complete the task. Record what the release checks establish and what still needs follow-up; a small rollout does not yet prove a lasting improvement for all users.
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.0: Verify each acceptance criterion one by one, with artifacts attached
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.1: Run the full suite in CI: tests, type-check, lint — all green
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.2: Human gate: you approve the production deploy (per team convention)
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.3: Deploy behind the feature flag; enable for 5% of traffic
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.4: Watch logs, error rate, and the audit table filling correctly
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.5: Expand only when agreed safety checks pass and sample users can complete anonymization; otherwise pause the rollout
m9.drill.exercises.6.items.6: Record release evidence and limitations; confirm who will compare the user outcome with the baseline and when
m9.drill.exercises.6.lens: Safe deployment and useful outcomes need different evidence. Keep release gates, then follow through on the problem the change was meant to solve.
m9.drill.exercises.6.prompt: 16:50. Final steward’s sequence for shipping the feature. Order it.
m9.drill.exercises.7.explain: The implementation can be correct without solving the customer problem. Early task completion is encouraging, but compare it with the starting point and gather enough observations before claiming improvement. Name an owner and a date, explain uncertainty, and adjust the solution if evidence disagrees. The miss log improves technical checks; user follow-up tests whether you chose the right solution.
m9.drill.exercises.7.lens: Responsibility continues after deployment: communicate what you know, arrange the next check, and learn from the result rather than declaring victory from green tests.
m9.drill.exercises.7.options.0.text: Yes. The tests pass and the error rate is unchanged, so the customer problem is solved.
m9.drill.exercises.7.options.1.text: Report verified behavior and what is still unknown. Agree that you and Mika will compare completion without support help against the baseline next week, and review user feedback. Record today’s near-misses and keep a named monitoring owner after handoff.
m9.drill.exercises.7.options.2.text: Send the agent’s implementation summary as proof that customers benefited.
m9.drill.exercises.7.options.3.text: The implementation is complete; whether it helps is now entirely the product team’s responsibility.
m9.drill.exercises.7.prompt: 17:15. The feature is live and operational checks pass. Mika asks, “Did we solve the customer problem?” What is the most responsible response?
m9.drill.intro: A day at LedgerLoop in eight decisions, from clarifying the customer problem to following up after deployment.
m9.drill.title: The Gauntlet · Eight checkpoints
m9.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: LedgerLoop is a small SaaS: invoicing for freelancers. 40,000 users, one Postgres database, a payments provider called Paybolt, and you — the most junior developer on a team of four, which today makes you the closest thing to an “agent steward” the company has. Your team lead is on a train with bad Wi-Fi. The product owner, Mika, messages you at 09:12:
m9.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: “Users keep asking to ‘get rid of’ their old invoices. Legal says we must keep records 7 years — but a user can anonymize their own invoices once they’re older than 90 days. Feels doable today? You’ve got the agent.” — Mika
m9.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: You have an AI agent, staging write access, production read-only access, and a team rule that migrations go through CI. The target is 17:00, not permission to skip approvals. First find out whether “get rid of” means reducing clutter or removing personal data. For this simulation, Mika then confirms that users want self-service removal of client details while retaining financial records. Agree to compare completion without support help before and after release.
m9.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: The Gauntlet has eight checkpoints: clarify the problem, specify the behavior, inspect the implementation, hold release safeguards, and plan follow-up. Six of eight passes the exercise. This is practice in judgment, not a professional certification or a substitute for experience.
m9.lessons.0.blocks.4.html: Keep three questions in view: are we solving the right problem, does the system behave safely, and how will we know the change helped? Use the technical lessons to justify your decisions, communicate uncertainty, and name who will check the outcome after release.
m9.lessons.0.title: Briefing: a day at LedgerLoop
m9.tagline: From an ambiguous customer problem to safe delivery and a plan to check the outcome.

ui.howLessons: Lessons teach one layer at a time and end with Judgment in practice: what decision does this help you make, what could go wrong, and how would you check the result?
ui.howProgress: Progress is saved in your browser. No account, no tracking, no server — this site is a folder you could own.
